Mr. Speaker, I wish to lay on the table two copies in English and French of the Canada Gazette, part II, statutory orders and regulations, issued on December 24, 1952.
I should also like to lay on the table a summary of orders in council passed during the period December 1 to 31, 1952.
I am sure the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) will be glad to know that there are only about a third as many as were passed in the month of December, 1951. That is due, mostly, to the establishment of government contract regulations and land purchase regulations, under which the powers of the governor in council are delegated in certain cases to the appropriate minister and, in other cases, to treasury board.
This action shows signs of improvement.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether or not the report from the commission on the Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project is available. If so, is it favourable, and is it the government's intention to go ahead with the project?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to answer the three questions separately. The information I have is that the printing of the appendices for the report will be complete on the 17th. We have asked if it cannot be advanced a bit so that we may be able to submit the report and the appendices to the Governor General and table them this week. I am not sure whether the printer will be able to comply with that request or not; but I fully expect that, if he cannot, they will be ready for tabling on Monday.
As to whether or not the report is favourable, I do not think I should answer that question until the report has gone to His Excellency the Governor General. I must confess that out of curiosity I read the first part of it, but I would not care to be further indiscreet about it or about action upon it.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION OF BUILDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. Can he say whether any definite decision has been taken .with respect to the construction of a building to house the national library?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION OF BUILDING
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I
should not venture to reply at once to a question in that form. There has been a decision upon a site for the national library, and an architect has been commissioned to prepare the plans for it.
In principle, the decision was made when the legislation was recommended to the house that there be a national library, when parliament saw fit, upon recommendation of the government, to appropriate the funds required for it. As soon as a decision to seek an appropriation is made it will be announced to the house.

subtopic: EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I gave him notice, but I am afraid it was a little late to be of much use to him. Then, I did not bring my own copy of the question to the house so, in that respect, we are both in the same position.
In view of the news reports which came from Paris and Bonn in the latter part of last week indicating that perhaps the European defence community arrangements were going to be altered in a far-reaching fashion-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL
speechtext: Question.

subtopic: EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Well, I was not directing it to you, but perhaps you would like to answer it.
In view of this, will it be necessary to revise the protocol that was endorsed and approved by this House of Commons last spring? Perhaps the minister would indicate

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Before I attempt to answer that question, which deals with a very important matter, I would wish to know whether the reported statements to which my hon. friend referred will result in any particular proposals and, if so, what these proposals will be. Before we get word of the proposals it is most difficult to say what effect, if any, they would have on the European defence community and the protocol to the North Atlantic treaty.
Replying to the latter part of the question,
I shall have to look up and see how many countries have ratified the protocol and I will let my hon. friend know as soon as I get that information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this question concerns matters in which the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Justice are all three interested, I believe it would be appropriate that I answer it. The answer to the first question is "no" and therefore the remaining questions are not applicable.
As this answer will appear to differ from a two-line statement in the Currie report tabled on December 15 last, I think I should state the facts in this connection so far as it has been possible to ascertain them. I make this qualification because a part of the information is based on statements secured by the police from Sergeant Young who is now in

the penitentiary and it is not possible to check all of them from official records.
In February, 1951, it was decided that an area in what is known as camp X at Peta-wawa should be cleared as quickly as possible. Teams and teamsters were needed, but only three farmers with their teams were found to be available for hire, even though they were to be put on the payroll at the highest rate authorized for tradesmen, namely, that of bricklayers at $1.50 per hour. As more were needed, Staff Sergeant Young hired horses on his own account from a civilian in Pembroke at $1 per horse per day plus feed and care, arranged with eight labourers to act as teamsters and had them placed on the payroll at $1.50 an hour as if they themselves were supplying the horses. The men kept their regular pay of 75 cents per hour plus 5 cents additional or 80 cents per hour and turned over the difference to Young.
Captain Baldock shared in this illegal profit, as he did in profits derived from certain other offences at Petawawa. There was no collusion between Young and the farmers who brought their own teams, and Young received no rebate from them. Both Baldock and Young have since been convicted and are at present serving penitentiary sentences.
The names on the payroll were the names of labourers who actually existed and who worked as teamsters. There were no false names on the payroll and no horses on the payroll. I am further advised that the customary income tax deductions were made against each one of these teamsters in accordance with his own personal family status.
What I am interested in learning is to whom the 70 cents a day, or whatever it was, was charged for purposes of income tax. Was it charged to the teamster or was it charged to the owner of the horse?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Deductions were made against each one of these labourers as if he were getting $1.50 an hour. The deduction was made in accordance with his own personal family status, whether he was single or married and had or did not have children, at the appropriate rates for that status. They have a credit against income tax which bears marks of the irregularities connected with the way in which the whole thing was engineered.
It sounds like a good deal for the owner of the horse.

Answered.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability

of introducing legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to remove the 4 per cent limitation from the section which makes provision for the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as everyone knows, there was in the former Income War Tax Act, and there is in the present Income Tax Act, a provision respecting the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes. This has been in effect since 1943. However, that provision is limited by at least three main conditions. In the first place, those medical expenses which can be deducted are only those expenses defined as such in the Income Tax Act. That definition was quite narrow at first. It has been broadened a bit from time to time but it is still, in the view of many of us, altogether too narrow. At any rate, that is one of the limitations upon the right to deduct medical expenses from one's taxable income before computing income tax.
A second condition which is attached to this provision is what is known as a ceiling. In other words, right from the start there has been an upper limit as to the gross or aggregate amount that any taxpayer can claim as a deduction for income tax purposes. That amount has been changed on two or three occasions. Indeed, a year ago the ceiling was raised so that it now is $1,500 for a taxpayer who is on a single basis and $2,000 for a taxpayer who is on a married basis, plus $500 per dependent up to a limit of four dependents, or a limit of $2,000 for one's dependents. That is the second limitation on this provision, namely, the ceiling, the present terms of which I have just indicated.
I said a moment ago that some of us are not satisfied with the narrowness of the definition of medical expenses. We feel that it should be much wider, and I want to make it perfectly clear that, although I believe that the definition should be broadened to include other drugs than those now covered, to include spectacles, hearing aids and other such items, nevertheless that request is not contained in the motion now before the house, for the simple reason that it is wise to make one request of this kind at a time.
With respect to the second condition, namely, that of a ceiling on the amount that can be charged, I support the principle of there being a ceiling. Prior to the change that was made last year I felt that the ceiling was not high enough, particularly in view of the increases that had taken place in the cost of medical care, but so far as I can see the figures that are set out now as a ceiling are more or less satisfactory. Therefore I am not asking for any change in that part of this provision.

I come now to the third of the conditions or limitations which is attached to the provision for deducting medical expenses. The third provision is what is sometimes referred to as a floor or, in other words, a stipulation that there can be deducted from taxable income only that portion of medical expenses which is in excess of 4 per cent of net income. When this provision was first written into the Income War Tax Act by Mr. Ilsley in 1943 that figure was 5 per cent. In 1944 the figure was reduced to 4 per cent. The story of that reduction is very interesting for, as I have pointed out on previous occasions, the budget resolutions of 1944 did not forecast any such reduction of the 5 per cent figure. There was, however, considerable clamour on the floor of the house for the wiping out of that floor or reducing it, and in response to the debate that took place on that occasion Mr. Ilsley came back later in the same session and reduced the floor to 4 per cent. However, there it has remained ever since 1944.
As hon. members know, the 4 per cent floor relates to one's net income, not just to one's taxable income. Thus, if a person is on an annual salary of $4,000 a year and is a married man, although his statutory exemption is $2,000-which means that he pays his income tax on only the other $2,000 -nevertheless, when it comes to computing his income tax and to ascertaining whether his medical expenses are of any help to him, he can enter on the income tax form only that portion of his medical expenses in excess of 4 per cent of the total of his income- namely, 4 per cent of $4,000. In that case the first $160 does not count. It is only the portion of medical expenses above $160 in that example that can be allowed as a deduction for income tax purposes.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the whole purpose of this resolution which is before the house relates to one point and to one point only, namely that 4 per cent floor. It asks that the 4 per cent floor be wiped out and that consideration be given to the necessary legislation to make it possible for taxpayers to deduct their medical expenses right from the first dollar up to the limits that are set out in the act. It is well known to all members of the house and well known to the people of Canada generally that that right-the right to deduct for income tax purposes right from the first dollar up to the limits specified-is accorded to donations to churches and charitable organizations. All we are asking for in this motion is that the same privilege, the same right that is accorded to contributions that are made voluntarily, be accorded
Income Tax Act
to those medical expenses which are met by taxpayers involuntarily or in other words because of necessity.
I am satisfied that there is wide support for this principle, for this request that medical expenses be put on the same basis as charitable donations, and that the 4 per cent floor be wiped out. In support of my contention that there is wide agreement with the request I am making, I remind the house that last year on March 26, 1952, this house passed unanimously a motion in my name which was similar to the one now before the house. I point out that the wording of last year's motion was slightly different from the wording of this year's motion and may I say immediately what the reason for the change is. The reason is that last year the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, who is now the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), in my view misinterpreted my motion in that he thought it was asking for something more than just the removal of the 4 per cent floor. He thought that I was asking for a complete removal of the ceiling as well. I have reworded the motion this year to make it clear that it is not asking for the removal of the ceiling. I would like to see the definition of medical expenses broadened but this motion just asks for one change, namely the removal of the 4 per cent floor.
Last year, once it was made clear on the floor of the house that that was all that was intended in the terms of my motion, the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance said in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that the motion was acceptable. As a result of that indication of acceptance by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, the motion received support in all sections of the house. Members on the opposition side were all in favour of it and a number of members on the government side, who on previous occasions were not so vocal, indicated their support last year by speaking to my motion. I refer particularly to the member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry), the member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), the member for Charlevoix (Mr. Mal-tais), the member for Skeena (Mr. Apple-whaite), as well as the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. All of them spoke and either directly or by inference gave support to my motion calling as it did on that occasion for the removal of the 4 per cent floor. As a result of that support in every part of the house, the debate was a rather short one and it ended by the motion being carried unanimously by this House of Commons.

Income Tax Act
I made it clear during the course of the debate that I knew what that motion meant. It meant that we were asking the government to give consideration to the advisability of making that change. No one in this House of Commons thought it meant that we were giving the government the kind of direction which it absolutely had to carry out; but it is also true, and we have made this clear in the house, that whenever a private member's motion asks for consideration of something toward which the government is not favourably disposed, that motion is either withdrawn by a government member at the request of the government, defeated, or talked out. I can find in the time that I have been here no record of a private member's motion asking for consideration of monetary or budgetary matters being passed unless the government was actually favourably disposed toward the substance of the motion. I think it was quite proper for the press of this country, Liberal press as well as opposition press, to assume as it did from the passing of that motion on March 26, 1952, that one of the changes which could be anticipated in the budget that was brought down on April 8 would be the elimination of that 4 per cent floor. As everyone knows, when we got that budget on April 8 there was no change whatsoever in the floor. The minister, on the other hand, did make a change in one other aspect of the legislation, a change which did not concern many of us too much-a change in the ceiling; but he insisted that the floor had to stand. The minister did not like it because we moved a motion of no confidence later on with respect to the matter and because we berated1 the government both inside and outside the house for ignoring the wish of parliament in respect of this matter.
I want to tell the minister today that for him to stand, if he chooses to do so, and say that the government carried out the terms of that vote and did give consideration to the idea is not good enough; and in my view it is not playing fair either with parliament or with the people of this country. The fact is that he went against the wish of this house. As the minister knows, the year before last I had a similar motion before the house relating to income tax deductibility. It dealt with the deductibility of trade union dues for income tax purposes. It is strange how things work in this parliament, because on that occasion my motion was defeated by a vote in this house on February 26, 1951, and it looked as though we were faced with a much longer battle to get deductibility for trade union dues. But, lo and behold, on April 10 of that same session-April 10, 1952 -when the Minister of Finance brought in

his budget he made provision for deductibility for trade union dues despite the fact the government majority had voted it down on February 26, 1951. Last year the tables were turned. The house voted1 for the idea on March 26-the idea of deductibility of medical expenses right from the first dollar- yet the government rejected that wish when the minister brought down his budget on April 8.
Well, I do not know what is going to happen to my motion today but I certainly hope-and perhaps one can express such a hope with a little more confidence in view of the fact that everyone expects an election before long-that whatever happens to my motion today the government will act on this reasonable request, this request for fair treatment, this request which all Liberals in this house supported last year, this request which newspapers from one end of this country to the other agree is fair and should be supported. I hope action will be taken on it in this year's budget and that the 4 per cent floor will be wiped out so that taxpayers will be allowed to deduct their medical expenses right from the first dollar in the same way as applies in the case of donations to charity.
Mr. Speaker, on previous occasions, and this has been up quite often, as ministers and other members on the government side know, I have placed certain figures on the record and I think I should put a few examples on today. It is necessary to keep putting these examples on the record because income tax rates keep changing and the examples put on the record a year ago do not apply now. I would like to take a few examples to indicate what happens as between medical expenses on the one hand and charitable donations on the other. The examples I have worked out are on the basis of the income tax rates now in effect for the year 1953. In other words, based on the rates in the latest office consolidation of the Income Tax Act, which are the rates for a full year as given in the columns that the minister placed on Hansard on April 8 last year, I find that a married couple without children, having an income of $200 per month or $2,400 a year, are treated in this way. If they make contributions to charity in the amount of $200 per year, their income tax saving as a result of the deductibility that is granted to them will be $38 for the year 1953.	1 have taken
into account both the general income tax and the old age security tax. The exact figures are these. Without any deductions, they would pay $68 general tax and $8 old age security tax, or a total of $76. But if they

give away $200 voluntarily, they will pay only $38 and thus get tax relief to the amount of $38.
If that same couple is faced with medical bills that amount to the same figure, $200, an amount they are required to spend whether or not they wish to do so, the tax saving they will get on the basis of this year's figures is only $19.76. The reason for the difference between the $38 of tax relief for the $200 given away voluntarily and only $19.76 tax relief for the $200 spent involuntarily on medical expenses is the 4 per cent floor.
Let me take another example. This time it is a married couple with two children where the total income is $300 per month or $3,600 per year. Their total tax at this year's rates, without any deductions, would be $253. If they gave away $300 in the course of a year, the tax saving which will be granted them under the law as it now stands is $63. But if that same couple with two children and that income has medical expenses of the same amount, $300 a year, their income tax relief will be only $32.76. How can anyone, Mr. Speaker, justify that discrimination? How can the minister justify the fact that he gives to people $63 of tax relief for giving away $300 but gives them only $32.76 of tax relief if they are faced with the necessity of spending that much on medical expenses?
I go on to the case of a couple with an income of $5,000 a year, again with two children. Their total tax, without any deduction, would be $568. If they give away $500 during the year, their tax relief for that generosity will be $120. But if the same couple, in the same circumstances, is faced with $500 of medical expenses, their tax relief is only $72.
In the name of simple justice, Mr. Speaker, in the name of simple elemental fairness, we are asking that these two things be put on the same basis. I am not complaining about the deductibility granted charitable expenses. I quite agree with it, and I support the idea. I support also the ceiling which the minister has imposed upon the amount of charitable donations for which one can claim tax relief. But how one can consider charitable donations in one way and medical expenses in another is beyond my powers to fathom, and I think is beyond the understanding of people in all walks of life in all parts of this country. I have done quite a bit of figuring in this connection because it strikes me that, in the words of the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), who spoke about this matter on a former occasion, it is the little fellow who would really be helped by our proposal that the 4 per cent floor be wiped out.
Income Tax Act
As a matter of fact, if you take the examples I have given, you will note that the percentage increase in relief that is afforded goes down as you get up into these upper brackets, which is as it should be. This would not be the case if there were no ceiling, but there is a ceiling and I have no quarrel with that.
Let us look now at the little fellow with an income of $2,400 a year who is married and has two children. How he gets by, none of us really knows. Supposing there is such a person and he has no deductions, his income tax for 1953 will be $17 general tax and $2 old age security tax, or a total of $19. If that man gives away $100 in the course of a year -how he could do it I do not know-he would have tax relief for the full amount of his $19. He would have no tax to pay, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would thus contribute $19 to him for his generosity in giving away $100. But if that man with $2,400 a year, with a wife and two children, is faced, as in most cases he probably is, with medical expenses of $100 a year, how much tax relief does he get? He gets 76 cents. Tax relief in the amount of $19 is afforded if he gives away $100, but only 76 cents of tax relief is afforded if he is faced with medical bills of the same amount.
Now, that illustrates the point that it is the little fellow who would really be helped by the proposal that we put before the house at this time. I could give other examples, as I have done on former occasions. Really, my only purpose in doing it again is to bring those simple examples up to date in the light of the tax rates that will apply for 1953.
However, I feel that I should perhaps deal with some of the arguments that have been put forth from the government side on former occasions in opposition to this measure. There have never been any arguments against it from the backbenchers on the government side. They support it, but on occasion the Minister of Finance and his former parliamentary assistant have opposed the substance of this measure. Indeed last year, although the parliamentary assistant seemed to favour it when he spoke on March 26, when he defended the government's failure to make the change in the budget he opposed this whole idea in substance.
One of the arguments put forward by those who oppose this matter in substance is that 4 per cent is an average amount that Canadians spend on medical expenses, and therefore there is no point to allowing that as a deduction. The first thing I want to say about the use of that phrase "average" is in the form of a story, and it happens to be a

Income Tax Act
story which I understand the minister himself once told to a gentleman whose loss we in this parliament and in this country feel very greatly. I refer to the severe loss we have sustained in the untimely passing of Dr. Clark, the former deputy minister of finance. His contribution to this country was an outstanding one. However, what came to my mind was a story I ran across some time ago. It is said that the Minister of Finance was one day having a little fun with his then deputy minister who was talking about averages. The story as I heard it is that the Minister of Finance asked Dr. Clark if he had heard about the fellow six feet tall who drowned in a lake the average depth of which was only five feet.

I want to say to the Minister of Finance, in line with the story that he himself told to the late Dr. Clark, that there is real point to the story; that it is no solution to people who are faced with heavy medical expenses to tell them that a portion of that is the average spent by Canadians. These people are still under financial strain because of these expenses. If there is to be any sense of fairness or justice in income tax legislation, I suggest that we should apply that fairness and that justice to these people.
The fact is that a great many people have no medical expenses at all during the course of a year. They are very fortunate. There are not many who go through life without

medical expenses, and in the years in which medical expenses do catch up with them we think that they should get the fairest possible treatment from the income tax authorities. But just as we would do that for people in the years when medical expenses do catch up with them, so we are concerned this year with the people who this year will be faced with heavy medical expenses whether the minister calls them average or not.
In connection with this whole talk about averages, might I point out that no such rule applies to charitable donations. Why do you apply one rule to medical expenses-

speechtext:
Well, whatever the figure is, I would like to see a substantiation of it. By the way, does that include all the tag days? If there is such a figure why does the minister apply the rule in one case and not apply it in the other? Similarly I might ask him, if he takes the view that income tax allowance is to obtain once you get over the average, why does he not apply it to the cost of living? I submit that $2,000, which is the total amount allowed a married couple today, is below the average cost of living. Therefore, if he is going to apply this rule of the average he must, without delay, raise the total exemption that is allowed both to single persons and to married people before they pay income tax. Therefore I strongly urge the minister to rethink his whole position about averages, to take to his own heart the story he told Dr. Clark, and not to press that phase of the argument any more.
Another argument put forward, of course, is that it would cost money; that it would deprive the treasury of a certain substantial sum of money. The figure put forward last year was in terms of $40 million odd. I am still not satisfied with the way in which that figure was computed. The then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance went into it in some detail on the floor of the house. He was also good enough to let me have the rather large chart on which the calculating had been done to obtain that figure. Basically, however, what seemed to me to be wrong with it was the assumption that to wipe out this 4 per cent floor immediately removed for income tax purposes 4 per cent of the national income of the country. The flaw in that argument, as I see it, is that there are a great many people who have no medical expenses at all in the course of a year, and many people who do have medical expenses are so far below the income tax exemptions that they do not get into the income tax paying class anyway. Therefore

on that basis I am not satisfied that the $40 million figure that the parliamentary assistant gave us is a correct one. But even if it is, I suggest to the Minister of Finance that his government has cried "wolf, wolf" about the loss of revenue and the danger of a deficit in his budget a little too often.
The people of this country are not impressed by that argument any more. They have been hearing those cries for some time. We cannot afford this, we cannot afford that, but somehow or other we continue to afford some rather expensive items, very expensive in some instances, and still the minister comes out with huge surpluses. The people of this country also know that although the government argues that there cannot be reductions in taxation in the years in between elections, come an election year and some very substantial reductions seem to be possible. Well, I am counting on the fact that everyone expects this to be an election year and that it will result in a change of thinking on the part of the minister with respect to this matter to such an extent that he will not be concerned about the amount of money involved in wiping out this 4 per cent floor.
But I say again, even if wiping out the 4 per cent floor does cost $30 million or $40 million by way of loss of revenue to the treasury, even if it has to be made up in some other way, is it not supposed to be one of the cardinal principles of taxation policy that it should be on the basis of absolute fairness? If that is the case, I am sure the people of this country agree with me, indeed I am sure all hon. members agree with me, that it is not fair not to allow those first dollars of medical expenses as deductions for income tax purposes.
I named a few moments ago the members of this house on the government side who rose to their feet in the debate last year and supported my motion. Some of them and some others met me out in the hall afterwards and spoke to me in terms that I am not used to around this house. They thought that I had done a good service to bring in that motion; that it was a very good idea. There is no doubt in my mind that it always had support amongst all the members of this house, even though government supporters did not say so until they had been given the cue from the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance.
As I have already said, it received wide support throughout the country in the press of all shades of opinion and amongst Canadians generally. Why was there that support? Well, because there is a good deal of essential decency in the hearts of members of parliament and in the hearts of the Canadian 68108-57i
Income Tax Act
people. That essential decency in these times says that when people are faced with medical expenses they deserve every possible consideration, they deserve fairness even from the income tax collectors. For my part and speaking for those of us in this group, we feel that even this is not enough. So far as medical expenses are concerned we feel, and we will come to it again later, there should be a complete program of national health insurance. This is only a drop in the bucket, only a step in the right direction, but it is a step in the direction of fairness, and I plead as strongly as I can with the house on this occasion not to backtrack, not to go back on what it did last year, but rather to pass this motion once again, and this time when this motion has been passed by this house I hope that the government will not say that negative consideration is sufficient, but rather that it will recognize that the house really believes in the principle of fairness with regard to deductibility of medical expenses, and that in this year's budget, which no doubt we will get just before an election, there will be a provision to wipe out that 4 per cent floor to permit people to deduct medical expenses right from the first dollar.
Before I resume my seat may I remind hon. members that I said in the early part of my remarks that the definition of medical expenses is really too narrow. You can deduct money that you pay to doctors, nurses and hospitals; you can deduct money that you pay for certain appliances; you can deduct money that you spend on certain specified drugs, but there are a great many things even in a strictly medical line which are not included.
It is also to be pointed out that when there is illness there are other expenses that face a family, and none of these of course is allowed. One of the ways in which the government could help to make up for the fact of the many expenses, extra help, extra food and all these things that come into the story of illness, is by at least removing this 4 per cent floor. May I remind the minister also that the provision he made two years ago to include insulin has, for many taxpayers, been inoperative because, while they may spend a good deal during the course of a year, if they do not get their expenditures over the 4 per cent level they receive no advantage at all. To describe as average the expense a person faces, when he has some illness which necessitates taking expensive drugs during the whole of his lifetime, is I suggest to be callous and indifferent to a very human situation.
So on all counts I suggest that never was a more reasonable request made to the House of Commons than that contained in

Income Tax Act
this motion. And, just as the house passed it last year, I hope it will pass it this year, and that the government will act upon the wishes of the house and make this change in this year's budget.

Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has pointed out, this motion is in substantially the same terms as the motion he presented to the house last year and which, as he has indicated, was passed by the house, and without any objection on my part.
I was not able to be present at the debate, but my then parliamentary assistant did discuss the matter and did indicate that the government had no objection to the passing of the motion.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext: Would you have made objection if you had been present?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
No, I would not, because I gave my parliamentary assistant instructions that I did not oppose the motion, and my reason for not opposing it was based upon the terms of the motion itself.
The motion offered at that time was in most respects exactly the same as that now before the house, namely:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to remove the four per cent limitation from the section which makes provision for the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes.
Now, in the light of subsequent events, 3 think I was wrong in taking the course I did take, in indicating to my parliamentary assistant that there should be no objection to the passing of the motion. I did it because I felt that it would be wrong and illogical for a minister of finance, at the time budget matters were under consideration, to refuse to give consideration to any proposal.
Every day I am receiving proposals from taxpayers as to how tax laws should be amended; and on that occasion I felt that, in the terms of the resolution as framed, it should be allowed to pass. I must confess that, in my innocence, I did not realize that it would be represented to the country as being the unanimous opinion of the House of Commons that this should be done.
We know how these resolutions are passed. I was not in the house that day, and I do not know what the attendance was, but I assume it was perhaps average-or perhaps even less than average, because it was a private members' day. In any case it was passed without objection from the government. But because in its terms it is, I think, clearly a

resolution which relates to the imposition of a tax, then, as we know, under our constitution proposals of that kind can be introduced only by a member of the government on recommendation of His Excellency.
Now, my hon. friend has said that this was not put before parliament as a direction to the minister. Well, I certainly think he is right in that; but he and his supporters have done their best to persuade the people of Canada that it was a direction.
It is all right to pass resolutions couched in these terms, relating to budget matters, if it is understood that they do indicate what they say, in the terms indicated, namely that the government should give consideration to certain matters. But the ultimate responsibility as to the fairness and the desirability of making these budget changes must rest with the government.
My hon. friend has, and quite accurately I think, outlined the history of this exemption, and the basis upon which it is granted. It was introduced by my predecessor, Mr. Ilsley, and the government of which he formed a part; and, as I have very good reason to know, he felt very strongly that provisions of this kind should contain a floor. There is a provision in the United States of, I believe, 5 per cent, and the ceiling there is somewhat different. I am told there is no deduction allowed in New Zealand or in the United Kingdom-but of course now in the United Kingdom, under the new health services, I would suppose that most medical expenses are paid out of the health fund.
I should like to take a few moments to indicate the philosophy behind the provision for a floor. In common with a good many other people in this country, and in the house, I have spent money during the last twenty-five years in raising a family. Unfortunately they are getting pretty close to a grown-up stage; but in the course of those years I have had to spend varying amounts in each year for dental care, for check-ups, for childhood diseases and so on. We have been extremely fortunate because none of our children has had serious illnesses, nor have my wife and I.
During those years however we have in each year paid out money in varying amounts. Perhaps sometimes it would be a few hundred dollars, and sometimes somewhat less than that-for these periodical check-ups, general child care and the like.
I see no reason in the world why I, or anybody else, should be in a position to deduct those normal expenses-and I prefer to use the word "normal" rather than "average". I see no reason why I should be permitted to

deduct those normal expenses from my income before calculating my income tax, any more than I should be entitled to deduct expenditures for clothing necessary to keep the children warm, or food necessary to keep them alive.
I think it is unsound, in principle, that normal living expenses of the individual should be paid out of income before tax.
That is the basis upon which the floor has been established. It may be, as I say, that the floor is too high. Perhaps it should be less than 4 per cent. It started out at 5 per cent, and it has been lowered to 4 per cent. I am quite prepared to look at that question again.
I am quite prepared to look at the question of whether there should be a floor at all.
However, I have endeavoured to indicate why I believe it is essentially fair that there should be some floor. Because one of the jobs that any minister of finance has to do is to try to spread the tax burden, which amounts now to something like four billions. He must try to spread the tax burden as fairly and equitably as possible among all taxpayers. If one taxpayer gets a concession or a deduction, then some other taxpayer must provide those moneys.
My hon. friend does not quarrel with the ceiling; he has never quarrelled with that. There may be a question as to whether the ceiling should be raised. I have a perfectly open mind as to that, and it is a matter of opinion. But quite obviously, both in my view and in his, there should be a ceiling. Otherwise the benefits of a deduction of this kind would be quite disproportionate as between those in the lower and others in the higher income tax brackets.
The question as to the definition and the eligibility of various expenses which would qualify for deductions is constantly under review. From time to time we have made additions in respect of the classifications of drugs and other expenses which can be claimed as deductions.
Those, then, are the principles upon which these deductions can be claimed. As I say, I have always felt that to be fair as between the different taxpayers in the country there should be some minimum below which a claim cannot be made for deduction of these expenses.
Then there is an added reason-and perhaps this is not an entirely compelling one: I refer to that of administration. I am informed that it would be extremely difficult-virtually impossible-to check claims for medical deductions if every claim, no matter how small, were eligible as a tax deduction. The case may not be completely analogous but I think
Income Tax Act
there is considerable parallel between the type of insurance which some of us take out having a $20 or $40 deductible provision. We decide that we will insure ourselves for minor losses in connection with our car or other insurable property and thereby get a much cheaper rate for the greater expenses.
The philosophy behind this actually is that it is quite within the capacity of the ordinary individual to pay the normal expenses incurred for medical care or attention, but when those exceed what can be considered as a normal amount then, and then only, should there be special relief. That is the principle which lies behind the law as it stands now.
I am not going to take a great deal more time discussing the principles underlying this law. The cost of granting blanket exemption of 4 per cent, as suggested by the hon. gentleman, would be quite heavy. I am told that if everyone claimed the 4 per cent deduction, that is to say, 4 per cent on income as indicated under the act, the cost would be something over $100 million. The estimate of some $40 million which was given last year would mean that a lot of people would not claim at all for medical expenses or would be substantially below the 4 per cent. In any case the cost undoubtedly would be substantial. It certainly can be argued that more equitable and widespread tax relief can be afforded in other ways.
At this time of the year budget matters are under consideration. I doubt if many new points could be brought up in connection with this matter.

Before going further I wish to say that personally I think it is an unfortunate circumstance, preventing the opposition from expressing their opinioifc in this parliament. It is a poor advertisement for parliament under the conditions that exist in this country at the present time.
I introduced this resolution at the last session, Mr. Speaker, and I spoke at some length on it. I know that quite a number of members were interested in speaking in support of this resolution. They represented all parties in this house but unfortunately, owing to the rules of the house, they were prevented from doing so. It is not my intention to speak at great length, Mr. Speaker, and I do not intend to repeat any of my previous arguments, but I do wish to deal with the matter from the point of view of the general demand for a policy on national conservation in this country and to indicate to the house the places where that demand comes from and the support for our proposal.
This is a subject in which I am particularly interested, Mr. Speaker, because not only have I been interested in conservation during the whole of my working life but I have practised conservation during the whole of my working period on my property in British Columbia. When speaking in support of this resolution last session, on March 26, 1952, I
Conservation
gave an historical review of the exploitation of natural resources throughout the centuries, and of the movement towards conservation in the United States and in Canada since the early days of this century, and stressed the need for establishment of a national policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use in Canada based on co-operation between the federal and provincial governments and the people of Canada. I suggested an outline of action that should be taken under such a national policy, including: 1. The establishment of sound standards of management and utilization of natural resources as a result of scientific advice and investigation;
2.	The establishment and financing of research work, and the co-ordination of these activities with the work of public organizations and individuals; 3. The development of a co-ordinated educational program aimed at the development of interest and co-operation of all Canadians from early school days on;
4.	A program of co-ordinated publicity that would utilize the facilities of the press, the national film board and public organizations;
5.	The establishment of a uniform law enforcement program in connection with the conservation of wildlife and other resources;
6.	The co-ordination of the activities of all governments, at all levels, with public organizations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when speaking in this debate last session, at page 834 of Hansard, the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) had this to say:
This is perhaps one of the most important subjects that this house could deal with.
We agree with him in that statement and we believe that he thinks it is of great importance-and we are glad to know that he recognizes the importance of this subject. However, I was somewhat disappointed, Mr. Speaker, to read in the Gazette of April 24, 1952, the following statement which is entitled "Resources effort 'great'-Winters":
Minister Says Policy Aimed at Development and Prudent Direction
Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., April 23-Resources Minister Winters said tonight "very great strides" now are being taken to develop Canada's natural resources, "and to manage them with prudence".
He told the Chamber of Commerce here in a speech prepared for delivery that "there is no lack of a general policy for conservation and resources development", and that there is frequent and cordial co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, and with industry in this field.
Mr. Winters said the best sign that there is adequate co-operation "is that the development of Canada's resources is going on apace-"
I was somewhat disappointed to read that statement in the press. First of all, I think the minister's "frequent co-operation between federal and provincial governments"

Conservation
should be "continuous co-operation". I do not think it is an argument in support of a satisfactory policy just to say that it is evidenced by the fact that development of our natural resources is going on apace. That is no assurance that the development of those natural resources is being carried out along sound lines and in accordance with strict conservation principles.
As opposed to the minister's opinion, Mr. Speaker, I want to quote the opinion of an outstanding scientist who has given a lifetime of study to the problem of conservation of natural resources in Canada. I am going to quote from a book entitled "Conservation in Canada" by O. M. McConkey, at page 12. In that connection I want to say that Mr. McConkey is professor of field husbandry at the Ontario Agricultural College and he is recognized across Canada as a great authority on this subject. I might say in this connection in passing that O.A.C. is my old college, and without a doubt it has made a great contribution during the years to agriculture in Canada, and even throughout the world. Personally, I would recommend to anyone interested in this subject the purchase of this book which, I believe, was published first early last year, and to study what Professor McConkey has to say. In any event, as opposed to the minister's opinion in this respect, Professor McConkey has this to say:
When we consider that as Canadian citizens we are guardians of our heritage of natural resources for future generations, we should establish permanent departments of conservation at federal and provincial government levels to co-ordinate and execute long-term plans of conservation of the nation's natural resources now.
Canada has a great opportunity to carry out a national plan of conservation. Canada is a new country. We can take warning from the mistakes of old civilizations where the resources of soil, water and forests have been destroyed. We can heed the lessons to be learned from sound forest and soil management in those nations that have survived over the centuries. We have all the advantages of modern science and the known techniques of conservation. At present we are exploiting our forests, soils, minerals, and oil at an alarming rate. The speed of exploitation will increase with the modem world's insatiable demands for raw materials for industry and war.
Now, this is his concluding sentence in dealing with that subject:
Do not let us be deluded by temporary prosperity. We should establish a long-term rational plan of conservation and administration of the natural resources of Canada now, before it is too late. We must not fail.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I want to contrast the opinion of that outstanding scientist, who has written a remarkable book and who has spent years of his life in studying this question as it applies to the Canadian
'Mr. Herridge.]
situation, with the remarks of the minister when addressing the chamber of commerce in Sault Ste. Marie.
I should like to give a few indications, Mr. Speaker, of the growing demand for, and support for, a national policy of conservation in Canada. I am going to give a few illustrations from the press. The first one I want to give is a portion of an editorial written by the editor of the Country Guide in the November issue, 1952. The editor of this paper, Mr. Harold S. Fry, a very noted agriculturist in Canada with wide experience in agricultural matters, and with a wide knowledge of Canadian conditions as well as public opinion in the country in which this paper circulates, had this to say-the editorial is entitled "Sensible Conservation Policy":
There is evidence that the provinces, who control our natural resources, are beginning to recognize, at long last, the need for a national conservation policy. Under the circumstances, the role of the federal government must necessarily be that of a co-ordinating agency, able to supplement the efforts of the individual provinces, where necessary, from the national treasury. The relationship calls for sound planning, good will and tact. The overriding interests of the nation, and the immediate interests of the provinces, must be harmonized to the advantage of future generations of Canadians, if we are to use these resources wisely.
Since world war I we have heard a great deal about the conservation of natural resources. Special departments of government have been set up to guard and develop them. Indeed, more than 40 years ago, Canada established the commission on conservation, which, after 12 years of successful and lasting work, was dismembered to serve political purposes and its* pieces distributed among several government departments. During the last quarter century, nearly all progressive countries have become increasingly concerned about the rapid rate at which the growth of population and of industry tends to use up resources. The United States, which produces close to half of the world's industrial output, is seriously concerned already about the rapid disappearance of its vast heritage of coal, oil, soil and underground water. European nations have recognized for many years the folly of wasting the resources which nature has provided. Canada's undeveloped resources are perhaps greater than those of any other industrial nation, in proportion to our population, but we owe this fortunate circumstance more to our delayed development than to our foresight.
There is another powerful and influential voice, Mr. Speaker, speaking in support of the need for a national conservation policy.
Now, that was an illustration from a paper circulated in the west. I want to read briefly from an editorial appearing in a paper circulated in Ontario. It is the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 21, 1952. This is what the editor has to say in an article on conservation entitled "We can control floods".
What this country needs is a national conservation board to organize and integrate the program made essential by floods, soil erosion, forest depletion and many other factors. Canada is the only

important nation in the civilized world with a government which gives no support to a sustained and general conservation program. It is spending a great deal on other things, which is money down the drain so far as permanent value is concerned. Those who are suffering from floods in western Canada have a substantial grievance against this government, which characteristically finds it convenient to do nothing about such matters until an election is about to take place. Floods do not await occasions.
There is another voice speaking in support of the necessity for a national policy of conservation.
Then, I wish to quote briefly from the Rural Co-operator of November 25, 1952. One paragraph in this editorial has this to say:
We must have a long-term conservation program and it must be introduced at once, before deterioration of our soils takes place. We would ask the provincial and federal governments to join in this program, a feature of which might be the establishment of numerous small dams on tributaries of our main watersheds and the development of farm ponds.
We believe the government of Ontario and our farm organizations must take action now to forestall a decline in the morale of our farm people and a repetition of the soil deteriorating practices of the thirties.
There is another voice, closely in touch with the farmers of Ontario, speaking in support of this policy.
I was interested, when reading the monthly letter of the Royal Bank of Canada of September, 1952, to read a most interesting article on the necessity for practising conservation in this country. I found it particularly well written, and written with a knowledge of the circumstances as they are today in this country. I want to quote one paragraph as evidence of support, and of the great awareness, of the need for this policy in Canada. It does not necessarily mean the spending of large sums of money by the federal government. It means effective leadership in order to coordinate the policies of the federal and provincial governments, and to create in the public mind a national conscience which will assure the preservation and conservation of our natural resources.
In this monthly letter I find this:
The activities of government at all levels should promote and assist the conservation practices which are to be undertaken by individuals, and government must accept the responsibility for necessary enterprises which are beyond the capacity of individuals. Government must, too, bring in regulatory measures, which are the rules of the game, just as necessary in conservation as they are in transportation, communication and other enterprises that affect the public welfare.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that we in the C.C.F. heartily support this proposal, but strangely enough when the C.C.F. proposes planning or regulatory measures some people refer to them as dictator's proposals. I 68108-5S
Conservation
believe that all sensible and intelligent people realize today that, in our complex civilization and in this complex economic development, there is no question but that if we are going to progress there has to be increased planning by government and increased exercise of regulatory power in these matters.
Furthermore, we have one organization in Canada which has paid a great deal of attention to this subject. I refer to the Agricultural Institute of Canada. For some years it has had a committee studying this problem. That committee was composed of some of the outstanding men in Canada in connection with agriculture, water resources, forest resources and other matters concerning our natural resources. They have done the people of Canada and the governments of Canada a great service in devoting their time and attention so closely throughout the years to this very important question. I want to deal for a moment with a brief the organization has presented to the government in connection with this problem. I shall have more to say about that when the bill proposed by the minister concerning water resources comes before the house. I just want to quote two paragraphs of the resolution, and then briefly from the policy that the Agricultural Institute of Canada recommends:
Whereas the Agricultural Institute of Canada developed, in 1948, a national soil and water conservation policy with the full approval of its members in all nine provinces, and presented this policy to the federal and all provincial governments at that time,
And whereas that policy strongly urged that all federal and provincial soil and water conservation policies should give recognition to the importance of placing the administrative responsibility in departments of agriculture,
And whereas the experience of the past fifteen years has proved that soil and water conservation are interdependent,
And whereas in 1935 the federal government, facing the serious national problems of soil erosion by wind, and the necessity of the development of water resources to minimize the problems of drought, passed the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and later the Maritime Marshland Reclamation Act, resulting in incalculable benefits to the areas concerned; and decided that the administration of this conservation activity should be the responsibility of departments of agriculture,
Be it resolved that the Agricultural Institute of Canada commends the government for its intention to provide legislation to deal with the very important problem of the conservation of Canada's resources; that a strong brief on soil and water conservation be submitted to the Prime Minister and the members of the cabinet.
And this brief was presented, Mr. Speaker. I am also pleased to see that there is one more step toward the development of a national policy on conservation in the legislation the government intends to bring before the house, but we in this group believe that this is too piecemeal an approach; that the

Conservation
conservation of all these natural resources should be co-ordinated and should be directed as the result of the development of a national policy by this government.
I want to deal briefly with the recommendations mentioned in this brief. The basic arguments of the submission made by the Agricultural Institute of Canada are these:
(1)	That efficient land use, which is dependent on soil and water conservation, is becoming of more urgent importance as the populations of Canada and of the world increase.
(2)	That there is need for a clearer and more comprehensive national policy of soil and water conservation than has been operated in Canada to date.
Naturally when you talk about a national policy on soil and water conservation you include forest conservation, because forest conservation is related to both. I continue with the recommendations:
(3)	That conservation and agriculture offers a highly complex problem, involving the services of trained personnel in many fields of agricultural art and science.
(4)	That for all existing, or potential, agricultural land, soil and water conservation are inseparable.
(5)	That the farmer must be considered the most important factor in the ultimate effectiveness of any soil and water conservation policy.
(6)	That the farmer can be helped most by those who know his problems the best.
(7)	That all experience shows the desirability of centring all administrative, planning and development responsibility in the field of soil and water conservation in departments of agriculture.
While dealing with this aspect of a national conservation policy, the brief deals particularly with soil and water conservation. I would like to deal briefly with the question of river bank erosion and river pollution. I did not have time to mention this at the last session, but I shall refer to it now because I think it is further evidence of the necessity for a national policy to cover all these fields. There is a great problem so far as river bank erosion is concerned in many places in Canada. It is a great problem on the Columbia river, which flows through the centre of my constituency. I understand that it is a great problem around lake Ontario and in other places in Ontario and other places. We have constant damage to river banks, in some instances to villages, towns and cities, and to valuable property, which goes on unceasingly but which fails to receive adequate attention. The menace, the threat, continues to be there because there is no national policy with respect to the problem of river bank erosion and also the pollution of rivers.
In my own constituency, Mr. Speaker, and in many parts of British Columbia, we had very heavy floods in 1948. The waters of the Columbia overflowed into the city of

Trail and caused thousands of dollars worth of damage; in fact the lower parts of the city could have been completely inundated had not the citizens of the district and the officials of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and all concerned worked very hard over a period of a week, using all the modern equipment that fortunately was available, to build a large dike to keep the river back. But the threat is still there. Any time the Columbia river rises above its banks there is a threat to the city of Trail, there is a threat to other communities along the Columbia river and a threat to farming land and so on. Nothing is done to remedy this because all governments continue to pass the buck, because we continue to operate under legislation that was drafted years ago, and because we fail to have a national policy so far as conservation is concerned.
I am told-I do not know whether I will get it quite correctly-that the constitutional position is something like this. I notice that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is listening. I went into this matter very carefully; in fact I read many letters that had been written about erosion on the Columbia river by the federal government or the provincial government or any organization or any individual since British Columbia entered confederation, and I can say that it has been a continuing threat and a continuing problem on the Columbia river and in the various communities since that time; and it continues to be a serious problem.
I understand that from the constitutional point of view navigable rivers are the property of the federal government. I see the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) shakes his head. If I am wrong in that respect I should like to be corrected.

So far as the use of the river for power purposes is concerned, I understand that is the responsibility of the provincial government. I understand that it is the kinetic energy of falling water that produces the power. Therefore, if the banks of the Columbia river overflow and damage the property of the city of Trail, since the city of Trail is the creature of the provincial government, it is actually the property of the provincial government damaging the property of the provincial government, and therefore the federal government has no jurisdiction. I understand that it goes something like that.

I am not a lawyer, and I may have got the matter slightly out of focus, but I do say that, Mr. Speaker.
For instance, the municipality appealed to the minister for assistance in building a river wall. There had been a river wall built in previous days, and I found that was done under some act during the depression that was for the general advantage of Canada; and they wanted it extended. I think the minister quite correctly said that it was not the government's place to deal directly with the municipalities; that it would be up to the provincial government to make representations. Therefore the city of Trail made representation to the provincial government. I understand that so far the provincial government has not made any representations to the federal government.
The point I wish to make is this. In my own constituency here is a continuing threat, which is a problem, and which has existed since British Columbia entered confederation. Because of the constitutional position, and because of our lack of a national policy on soil, water and forest conservation, governments continue to pass the buck, property continues to be destroyed, and nothing permanent is done about it.
I do think that is one problem that the federal and provincial governments should handle. It has to be met. Whatever is done has to be paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. In my opinion we need a policy that would cover a situation of this kind, which exists in many places in Canada.
The same thing occurs with respect to the pollution of our navigable waters. There is no policy concerning the prevention of the pollution of those waters. Expansion of industry means increased pollution of many of our great rivers. This situation indicates the need for a national policy to protect our waters.
I shall not say more on that at this time, because I am sure there are other members in the house who will have something to say on the resolution. Before passing on, however, I must pay tribute to the Department of Agriculture for the good work that has been done by that department throughout the years under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. The only thing required to make that act fully effective is its extension to all provinces in Canada, so as to bring the administration of the act within the terms of a national policy.
What we require more than money at the present time is leadership and co-ordination which will bring about the building up of a
Conservation
national consciousness in support of that policy. I wish to pay tribute to the science service of the Department of Agriculture. This service undertakes investigations in respect of various pests, insects and forest diseases. I know that in my district the science service has conducted some very interesting and worth-while studies. The work they do for the forest industry of British Columbia is highly appreciated by that industry.
All I suggest in the resolution is that all these good works should be placed together in a national policy so as to co-ordinate the activities of all these people so they may work in one direction with one general purpose and objective.
In addition to the organizations, persons, editors and other organizations I have mentioned, I would point out that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture supports a national policy of conservation. The Canadian Congress of Labour on various occasions has expressed strong support of a conservation policy in this country. The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Canadian Forestry Association, many other organizations and thousands of people who are interested in this subject are urging the government to establish a national conservation policy. I cannot take time to mention many individuals, but I do wish to refer to two or three. I would refer first to a gentleman in Montreal, Mr. J. L. Van Camp of the Canadian Forestry Association, who has done a great deal of excellent research work and writing in connection with the conservation of our forests and water resources. I would draw attention particularly to a pamphlet he put out recently under the heading "Water is a Forest Product". This is an excellent pamphlet, and I should like to see it distributed generally throughout the schools of this country. Men like Mr. Van Camp are working behind the scenes and making a study of the problem so as to provide information which would serve as a basis for the establishment of a national policy on conservation.
Then in this connection I would mention Mr. A. Koroleff, who has done much research work in connection with water and forest conservation. I would advise anyone interested in the forest industry to secure a copy of his book entitled "Stability as a Factor in Efficient Forestry Management", published by the Pulp and Paper Research Institute of Canada. It is one of the best books on the subject to be found in recent years anywhere on the North American continent.
Then again I must pay tribute to Professor McConkey of the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph for his book "Conservation in

Conservation
Canada". I would recommend it to all members on all sides of the house. It represents years of thought and investigation.
Before concluding I should like to quote once again from Professor McCohkey's book, where he says:
The Canadian people have been blessed with a great and beautiful country, fairly rich in natural resources. It is ours to use wisely, and to hand on to future generations without waste.
We need a change of mental attitude from the prevalent materialistic thought of getting rich quick through the exploitation of our natural resources to that of conserving and improving our resources- a love of our land. Learning about conservation is not enough. What is desired is the development of a conservation consciousness, which results in changed behaviour. The ideals, knowledge and skills of the school children of our country will have much to do with what happens to our land and its resources now and in the future. Conservation is a primary obligation of Canadian citizenship.
I should like to see the government give a lead in this direction. He continues:
Education in conservation is an urgent need of our Canadian people at all levels, through primary and secondary schools, colleges, universities and adult education.
What I am saying this afternoon represents the viewpoint of the C.C.F. It represents the viewpoint the C.C.F. has presented continuously throughout the years. In its program, in its literature, on the public platform and in the House of Commons the C.C.F. has proposed consistently that a partnership of federal and provincial governments should take over the development and conservation of our resources in the name of the people. Then profit would be no longer the main incentive; proper care and economic development could ensure a higher standard of life for the Canadian people in perpetuity.
As I have said, conservation is the practice of keeping the economic activities of the nation, the activities of man, in harmony with mother earth and with nature. There is one thought I wish to express before taking my seat, and that is that interest in the conservation of natural resources produces cultural and spiritual values; perhaps I should say intangible values. They are immeasurable, and cannot be counted. History proves that those who love the soil make good citizens. We do not find any amount of violent crime in the country, in the rural parts of Canada. We do not find much delinquency in the rural areas. Those conditions are found in much greater degree in our cities. So far as the record is concerned, we find that wherever people are interested in their natural resources, are interested in the soil and are interested in nature, they can be accepted as those who are responsible citizens and with the greatest degree of stability.
IMr. Herridge.l
For years the C.C.F. has preached the doctrine of the conservation of human and natural resources. Once again the soundness of our policy is being demonstrated by the increasing demand for the planned development of natural resources across Canada. There has been a wider and wider support of the ideas put forth and expressed throughout the years by members of this group.
Great progress in the conservation and planned development of natural resources has resulted from a national policy based upon the co-operation of federal and state governments in the United States. Prior to the development of a national policy in that country, little progress was made in that respect. I think a careful reading of the records of that country will indicate that its development has come about through the co-operation of federal and state governments, as well as that of organizations and individuals in that country. When that took place they began to make some real progress in preventing the further deterioration of their vast natural resources.
We in this group believe that Canada needs action now on this great question. That action can come only as the result of effective leadership by the federal government, based upon a national policy such as we suggest. More and more Canadians subscribe to the creed of a Nigerian chieftain who said:
I conceive that the land belongs to a vast family, of which many are dead, few are living, and countless numbers are still unborn.
We in this group urge the government to give the Canadian people an opportunity to practise this philosophy by means of a national policy on soil, forests and water conservation and land use for Canada.
