an ever-growing population with water is daily becoming more critical. The same thing can be said to a lesser degree of the two northern Pacific states. Even in British Columbia, where there is such abundant rainfall, the incidence of drought this year is a warning that we cannot let go unheeded.
Coming now to the part of the country where I live, the rural section of old Ontario, it has been estimated that in order to provide adequate forest cover for farm land at least 14 per cent of the land should be under such cover. In many counties and townships in old Ontario and old Quebec, that part of the two central provinces south of the clay belt, less than 5 per cent, in some cases only 3 per cent, of the land has adequate forest cover. In other words we have depleted our forest cover to one-third of that which is considered to be desirable for a balanced economy by forestry engineers and agronomists, I believe they are called, who understand the business of land use. There is a great temptation for more and more land to be put to the plow and cropped, particularly when prices are high and when specialty crops such as tobacco command extraordinarily good prices, and it is understandable that more and more land should have its forest cover removed.
| I want to make a suggestion to the government. I suggest that we have an optimum *of 14 per cent forest cover over our agricultural farm belt in southern Ontario; and that the federal government, through grants in aid to the province, should work out with the province, and the province in turn with the county and township governments, a method whereby the local governments could be recompensed for the taxes lost on land given over to increased forest cover. My suggestion is somewhat along this line. If a municipality had 5 per cent of its land under forest cover and it was desirable to increase it to three times that amount, and if the taking of an extra 10 per cent of the land out of agricultural use and putting it under trees would decrease the tax revenue of the municipality, the federal government together with the province should work out a method by which the municipality could be recompensed for the loss of revenue caused by increasing the forest cover.
I want now very briefly to mention the timber industry as such and not in connection with forest cover. I want to quote a report which appeared about a year and a half ago written by John D. Gilmour, B.Sc.A., who also has a B.Sc. in forestry. He is speaking

with regard to the use of our Canadian forests, and the title of the pamphlet is "Canadian Forest Policies are All Wrong". The first three paragraphs of his pamphlet are as follows:
Canadians should check up on the management of their forests. Appalling deterioration has taken place during the last 50 years-a very short time in the life of a nation-and unless forest policies are changed speedily this country faces Complete forest bankruptcy.
This appeared in the Canadian Banker, the periodical of the Canadian Bankers' Association; and he says:
It is well that bankers, who are most vitally interested in Canada's long-term future, should interest themselves in forest management. The forest industries constitute the largest industrial group in Canada, contributing enormously to our domestic economy as well as to the maintenance of foreign trade and the earning of U.S. dollars.
Although many among the best-informed Canadians despair of the forest future, because the problem is mainly a political one and wrong propaganda has for many years been at work upon the public, there is time yet to apply statesmanship and courage to find the right solution. Good examples are afforded by other countries.
I do not profess to know anything about the problems of forest management but I am quoting this article by an expert and I think he hits the nail on the head fairly well when he says the situation is political.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are we frightened of? What possible problem are we frightened of politically with regard to our forests? The major industry in Canada today is that of forest products; yet we have articles written
and published in the most conservative____with
a small "c"-periodicals such as the Canadian Banker saying that our whole forest industry faces bankruptcy. It is a problem which this house cannot fail to take most seriously.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that one of the worst criticisms which could be levelled against parliament is that in all the years I have been a member, fourteen of them now, the committee on mines, forests and waters has never met. Would it not appear that here is a problem-a technical problem if you like, but a vital problem-affecting our whole economy, about which we have done nothing. There have been resolutions like that of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge); there have been private bills similar to the one I brought in some years ago with regard to pollution; but the committee has never met to discuss this very vital factor in the economy of our country, the soil and the forest cover.
You would think that this house was not interested. You would think that this was something of minor importance. The very feeding of the world and the economy of our

whole nation stems from the soil, and the forests stem from the soil. With the horrible examples of erosion, of flooding, of dust bowls, and the shocking example on this continent of the Pacific coast situation, as far as I know for nearly a quarter of a century we have never once thought it worth our while as members of this House of Commons to call that committee together and bring in experts to see if something could not be done.
These things are not likely to produce headlines. There is nothing startling in increasing forest cover, and erosion, except in times of great and sudden flooding, is a slow thing. It does not rage like a fire, though when the floods come their devastation is just as quick and just as complete. On this question of soil rests our security, our ability to build our population, our ability to do our duty as a world power, but we let it go. We let the soil become more friable, we let our forests burn, we let our rivers erode, we pollute our streams, and we destroy our wildlife. Why, Mr. Speaker? Why do we do these things? Why do we allow these things to happen? Why do we sit here and let our land be slowly consumed by this monster? I do not know.

For nearly two years I have tried to get the minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan to co-operate with the P.F.R.A. in the draining of the area between the Saskatchewan river and the Carrot river. There is a delta
Conservation
there which extends from the Carrot river to The Pas. It is a wonderful piece of land which could be developed and put under cultivation. The work would cost too much for the province, but not in co-operation with the federal government. I have tried to persuade two ministers to co-operate with the federal Department of Agriculture to get this great scheme for the Carrot river delta started. The hon. member for Churchill commenced working on the scheme at the same time I did. He has reached the point where Manitoba is talking of an agreement to take care of the Manitoba side of the delta.
I believe it is quite unfair to state that the federal government is not taking care of our land in western Canada. The P.F.R.A. in connection with community pastures, and the removal from cultivation of the dried-out area which has been put back to grass, has proven to be an outstanding piece of legislation. There has been co-operation with the provinces, and it has proven a great thing for western Canada. We are urging that the
P.F.R.A. develop more land of this kind in the different parts of the three western provinces. It is good grazing land, but it is unsuitable for agriculture because it has periods of drought. We may go back a long way and say that it was a certain government's fault that this land was ever thrown open for homesteading. The land did provide a living for many people for a good long time. The P.F.R.A. has taken it over and is putting it back where it belongs, as grazing land.
The problem with regard to land and water conservation in the north is far different from the problem which we have here. As I have said, we have thousands of acres of small bush in my constituency. Since 1942 we have put about 50,000 acres of this bush land under cultivation, and it is now producing all kinds of grain. Some farmers are allowing their land to go back to pasture and some, on the advice of the P.F.R.A., are planting trees around their farms to make snow belts. There is no doubt that in time the northeast part of the province of Saskatchewan will do its share in providing food for the rest of the world.
Some years ago at one of the food conferences a member stated that there was not sufficient arable land in the world to give everyone in the world an American standard of living. I believe that is something we have to take into consideration. I believe one of the worst sights I have seen came to my attention in the province of Ontario. I am a great lover of the soil. I love to see the plow

Conservation
turn over the soil. I do not like to see a bulldozer removing good soil. Two or three years ago in the township of Etobicoke I saw bulldozers digging cellars in very good earth. If anything hurt, that did. I went up to the contractor and said, "Surely it is time we realized that there are thousands of acres upon which we can build houses without tearing up this good soil." He said, "This is going to be part of the city of Toronto." I believe it is time they got together and moved part of the city of Toronto up into northern Ontario, where it is possible to build houses without interfering with the food production of the country.
Some day we will realize that we have to take care of the good land the Lord has given us. I am sure that with good tillage, good care and good organization a great deal of land could be conserved. I am satisfied that we should co-operate with the provinces. In fact I would go this far, and say that in conserving land and water for the good of the people of Canada, we should not listen too much to the provinces. Our first duty to the people of this country is to provide food. It will not be long before the North American continent will need all the food it can grow. It will not be very long before there will be 185 to 200 million people in the United States, and it will not be long before there will be 20 or 30 million people in Canada. Then our wheat fields in western Canada, which are called the bread basket of the Anglo-Saxon people, will look pretty small to 200 or 300 million people. I am in favour of our joining together in Canada and co-operating to see that every bit of our land and every bit of our water are taken care of.
We need the South Saskatchewan dam; we need that lake of water across Saskatchewan. I am not going to go into that now; we can say more about it later on, but we need that. Five hundred thousand acres can be utilized on our western plains. That would feed a lot of people.
In closing I wish to say there is no reason why the Saskatchewan government cannot cooperate with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act administration and try to make that Carrot river delta as good a producing piece of land as the Portage plains.

Mr. Speaker, I find there is much in what the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) has just said with which I can agree. The last two or three resolutions that have been produced by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) have been supported by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson)

and the hon. member for Mackenzie. This indicates that it is a subject on which there is very little political difference. I notice that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) applauds. It may be that because of the Christmas spirit we are going to have a happy time for the remainder of the session. However, I am not so sure of that.
I am going to try not to repeat what has been covered in the speeches that have been delivered by the previous speakers, because I know we are all in unison, as the hon. member for Mackenzie has said, in our belief that people must be fed. We are conscious of the fact that the population of this world is increasing steadily and that millions of people are starving to death every year. We are also conscious of the fact that 60,000 more people are being born every day than are dying. We are also conscious of the fact that it has been estimated that the deserts of the world are increasing by 50,000 acres every day, and it is almost terrifying to try to comprehend just what it means.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has moved this resolution which involves conservation of soil, soil use, forest and water conservation. I am not critical of it. It is so important that we can all agree with it. In fact each feature of the resolution is so important that they all seem to be smothered by the tremendous consequences that are involved. Therefore I am not going to enlarge on what has been said in that regard, except to say that I am in full agreement with it. Judging by the attention that has been given to the matter by those who were in the house I know that we can all agree. It is not a case of party politics; it is not a case of criticizing this government particularly for not having done more than they have done in the last number of years, or of criticizing any particular province; because in fairness I know that the dominion government has its sphere of responsibility. As much as they may intrude on provincial rights, particularly by using their taxation powers occasionally, at least they do respect the old basic principle that the provinces are responsible for civil and property rights, and they do not like to intrude too far.
For many years, as you know, Mr. Speaker, I have strongly supported our policies on agriculture. I have been keenly interested in agriculture, but I have been concerned to see so much money set aside for agriculture in this dominion. I am not critical of that. In fact I realize that there is no one in this house who has not at some time or other said that agriculture is the basic industry,

the backbone of Canada, and so forth. We all know it is important; but I feel that sometimes we overlook other more important industries. Therefore I am not going to deal with water conservation, land use or the soil itself, because we know that the greatest God-given heritages we have are the first six inches of soil and the forests. Forestry is important. For many years it has been more important in your province, Mr. Speaker, than agriculture. In fact I think it is more important yet in that rich province to the east. Almost every province in Canada is vitally concerned. Forestry and forest products generally, as the previous speakers have said, have been to some extent overlooked. There is no industry in this dominion, Mr. Speaker, that gives so much to the national revenue of this country and gets so little out of it. No industry in Canada pays as much in taxes into the national revenue as does the forest products industry of this dominion, and no industry of any importance gets so little from the dominion by way of assistance.
In agriculture we have the central experimental farm and other farms supported by the dominion government; we have agricultural services supported by the government; we have all sorts of assistance from the dominion government running into hundreds of millions of dollars over the years. Again, Mr. Speaker, I do not say this in a critical mood of the present government. It has been the way of governments in Canada down through the years. So far as that is concerned no party in this house, neither the party forming the present government nor those who sit in opposition representing Her Majesty's loyal opposition, has any monopoly on how little it has done for the forests of Canada.
As has been said by the hon. member for York West today, we have smugly gone along and taken it more or less for granted. We have had all sorts of parlour criticism about what has been happening to our forests. I am not going to speak on that, or of what reforestation and keeping the ground covered with forests means to water levels. Every hon. member knows that very well. He who runs may read.
Not so long ago I read an article which said it has been estimated that a thick reforestation of five acres will raise the water table from 3J to 4J feet on fifty acres of land. Therefore it has a great effect on our whole national life, on climate, streams and all the rest of it. We know how streams have dried up even in our time because of lack of forests; and I do wish to mention the importance of the forest products industry of this dominion.
Conservation
As I have said, it is Canada's leading industry. It pays more into the treasury of this dominion than any other industry. It is first in the amount of wages paid in Canada. It is first in the employment of our people. It is first in value of exports to the United States, and plays a leading part in our trade with that nation. It stands first in importance in world trade. Our tremendous forest resources are of vital concern to the Canadian economy. No similar number of people anywhere in the world have at their disposal the vast forest resources we have in Canada.
I am pleased to speak on this occasion.
I hope no one will suggest that I am speaking only because I am personally interested in this industry. It will be kept in mind that I am also interested in agriculture, and have been interested in it all the days of my life. Whether or not we get more votes on the hustings than do the government supporters who would look for the support of the farmers, we must not forget that the forest industries of Canada are vital to the economy of our nation. They were of great importance during the years of depression, and all down through the years have been of great value to this nation.
Despite high grain prices, I would remind the house that exports from the forest industries of Canada have for several years brought in more foreign dollars, chiefly United States dollars, than has agriculture. Perhaps there are only a few people who realize the truth of that statement. We have been in the habit of accepting agriculture as our chief industry, from the standpoint of the income it produces.
I know there will be those who will say that our forests are being depleted and ruined. There are policies of reforestation that are sound in principle and should be proceeded with. I give my support to this resolution because it brings a matter of great importance to the fore, to the attention of the house and the government, and gives the government an opportunity to sit in with the provinces. I am not critical of the fact that the present government has not gone all-out in a program of road-building, fire protection and protection against disease in our forests. That is not the function of the federal authority; rather it is that of the provinces.
However, it is a matter of vital national importance that, no matter what party may be in power, the forest industries should be given careful attention. When I refer to the forest industries I mean, of course, lumbering, logging and all those other occupations involved. All governments in Canada should consider the forest industry as of paramount

Conservation
importance, even surpassing agriculture. Thus far, this has not been done.
I have only a word to say about the utilization of forests. I know there are those who will say that the forest industries are depleting and ruining our forests. They will say that those who are interested in forestry are proceeding in a reckless and haphazard fashion. Well, that may be a popular, parlour criticism, but I suggest it is wrong. It is just as nonsensical as if I were to tell some of my friends from western Canada that they should not cut down a beautiful field of golden wheat because those of us from eastern Canada would like to look at it. It would be just as foolish for us to say that it would be a shame to cut down that wheat. The difference is that it takes 50 or 75 years to develop a crop in the forest, while in the wheat field it takes only a few months, perhaps six or eight. Sometimes it takes longer than others. In Ontario, where we grow fall wheat, we think it takes about a year to get a crop.

It may be that the hon. member who interrupted first comes from a pretty rich district.
I have made these observations in passing so that the matter may be placed before the house fairly. This is a subject familiar to many hon. members. Indeed I know the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as well as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) know about the great forest industry of their native province. But this industry is divided into different spheres.
I mention this feature in passing because, after all, trees are like people. They are born; they blossom; they come to full fruition. Then they begin to get a little gray on the top, the foliage becomes somewhat scarce. Eventually they begin to dry up, and finally they fall down and die, returning to the earth.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: A sad story.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Yes, it is a sad story; and, young as you are, some day you will realize the truth of it. There are some people who believe that because we have a beautiful forest it should not be cut down. I would commit the same folly if I were to say that because I have a beautiful crop of wheat on
[Mr. Rowe.l
my farm it should not be cut. There is no harm done, if these crops are properly harvested.
How are our forests harvested? Twenty-five per cent of the forest products are used to produce logs and lumber, pit props, railway ties and the like. Then from 23 to 24 per cent is used for fuel, to keep our houses warm. About 22 per cent of the total forest depletion in Canada is used by the pulp and paper industry. It is interesting to point out that a greater proportion of our forests is lost through fires and insect pests than is used in the great sawlog and lumbering business or the great pulp and paper industry. Then more of our forests are lost from lightning and disease than the amount used to keep our houses warm.
We should keep these thoughts in mind when we consider what is happening in our forest industries. It is not my intention to speak at great length, but I do urge that the government give the matter consideration. True, this is a private member's resolution; but in the interests of soil conservation, water conservation, and everything involved in these great forest industries, I urge the government to give consideration at the earliest possible moment to the setting up of a dominion-provincial conference to study this problem.
Someone may ask what can be done. I know this government seems to be getting more modest every day. Perhaps it would hesitate to infringe upon civil and property rights in the provinces to any greater extent than it already has. I ask the government to approach this subject as one that is fundamental to our economy, one that is as important as agriculture. The whole standard of living of our people depends upon what is involved in this resolution. Soil utilization and water conservation, employment and wealth-all these things are involved.
I am not one who believes that the forests of Canada are going to be depleted; not at all. I have made personal observation of our forests being harvested over several years. In one area, within a period of 20 years, I have seen half a dozen trees growing for each tree cut down. We know that in Ontario one of the large pulp and paper mills is now going over the very same ground from which it harvested trees 50 years ago. The same is true of the province of Quebec, the province of British Columbia and other places. The forest wealth of this dominion is tremendous, but only about one-third or one-quarter is being utilized. The other two-thirds or three-quarters is growing up, falling down and dying as I have tried to describe.

I believe there is a great field for the closest possible co-operation between the provinces and the dominion, as previous speakers have urged this afternoon. I do not think it is a waste of trees, if they are properly harvested, to cut them in order to keep people warm. I do not think it is a waste of trees to cut them in order to provide permanent employment for thousands of people. More people are employed by the forest industries of this dominion than by any other industry. I know of several such places, but there is one with which I am familiar where the third generation is working in the same plant. If the trees are properly harvested, if there is proper management, if the proper interest is taken by the public and government to protect our forests, not so much from being improperly cut and harvested as from insects, disease and fire, then there will be perpetual production and perpetual employment.
About three or four years ago I had the opportunity of visiting a mill in Sweden. At the front of the mill was a stone on which it was indicated that it had been there for 600 years. I asked the manager what it meant, where the stone came from. He laughed and said, "The older it gets the more we think of it, because everybody asks about it. This was a saw mill 600 years ago." That company was cutting trees on the same area. That is why it is like agriculture, only it takes 65 years for the one crop to grow while it takes only 65 days for the other crop to mature.
In our provinces it has been left to the different companies to do their own roadbuilding. These companies have to build roads and clean streams in order to make them navigable and in shape to take out the lumber. Roads are necessary in order to get the men in and the lumber out. Quite often it will be found that there is a gap of 40 or 50 miles between the roads of one lumber company and those of another just over the horizon. When a fire starts and is discovered by the fire rangers in their towers it is quite often found that it is inaccessible by road. Millions and millions of dollars have been spent by the forest industries of this country in the building of roads. Some companies have two or three hundred miles of roads on their limits. These are necessary in the carrying out of their operations.
It is true that a great amount of our forest wealth is being used. Every day the sun rises one hundred acres of Canadian forests are used to print the New York Times. I am mentioning only one, but I could mention other newspapers in the United States which
Conservation
are using just as much of our newsprint. It is said that is ravaging our forests, but the fact is that this wood is being cropped and is providing a lot of employment. These operations can be perpetuated.
This matter transcends Canadian politics; it is something indigenous to Canadian national life and our standard of living. I urge the government to give some thought to this problem. Probably it cannot be done by means of this resolution because with all due respect to the hon. member who has introduced it-I thank him for bringing it up at this time-it is almost too comprehensive; it covers almost too much. Perhaps he might say that one issue is involved in the others but I urge that there should be the closest co-operation between the dominion and provincial governments.
I urge the government to consider giving grants in aid to the provinces. I know they do not like to give money to provinces to be spent by someone else, but perhaps there could be a commission or a joint management scheme arranged to handle this assistance for road-building. I urge the government to give consideration to evolving a plan by which our forest rangers and fire fighters will be able to get to any trouble that may develop.
We sometimes blame the government for not having enough forest rangers when we see a fire ravaging a whole mountainside, but it must be remembered that a great many fires are due to lightning. This happens in districts where the trees have been infested with worms or disease and are so brittle that they almost explode when struck with lightning. The men who fight these fires should be able to get to them.
A scheme of roads in the forest areas of the different provinces would be of great assistance, and I urge the government to give some thought to providing grants in aid to the provinces in order that assistance may be given to an industry which provides more revenue for the national treasury of this dominion than any other industry, yet is receiving less because of what might be termed constitutional responsibilities.
There should be a conference between the provinces and the dominion to clarify what might be termed constitutional technicalities. The provinces are directly responsible for civil and property rights, but this great forest wealth involves our soil, our water tables and our national economy. So much is involved in this issue that the dominion government owes it to the Canadian people to give greater consideration and more attention to our great forest industry.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I did not take advantage of this opportunity to support my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). The resolution he has on the order paper is pretty broad, and one could wander very far afield. However, I am not going to do that this evening. I have two points I want to make that are germane to the resolution, and I am going to stick to those two points. They arise out of a memorandum I have in my hand from the Nova Scotia fanners' association.
During the recess, in fact on January 7, this association held a meeting in Halifax to which they invited all the Nova Scotia members of parliament for the purpose of putting before them certain matters that are bothering the Nova Scotia farmers' association. I was not able to attend their meeting because I was tied up with other matters, and told them so; but I received a copy of a memorandum from them which no doubt all other members from Nova Scotia received. In order to lay the premise for my few remarks I am going to quote a paragraph from the memorandum which is relevant to the resolution now before us. The memorandum deals with several other matters having to do with the problems of agriculture in that province, but they can be dealt with at a time when a subject is before the house to which they can be related. The paragraph I wish to read from their memorandum is as follows:
For a number of years our provincial and national organized farm groups have been concerned with instituting some type of conservation of our soil, water and forest resources. In a recent reference made through the speech from the throne, it was intimated that such a program would be developed and administered under the Department of Resources and Development. We feel that any program of conservation which will be dealt with through provincial and national channels, and will ultimately concern the farmers of this nation, must be under the jurisdiction of trained men in the profession of agriculture working in close cooperation with our farmers, and we urge that serious thought must be given to this before our federal legislation is proclaimed. Soil and water conservation are inseparable and the experience of other countries in endeavouring to administer similar legislation in departments other than agriculture has left much to be desired.
I am in agreement with that statement. The speech from the throne did indicate that conservation measures such as are mentioned in the memorandum were being considered and would be undertaken by the Department of Resources and Development. I agree with the statement in the memorandum because

I believe that particular function belongs to the Department of Agriculture. At the present time the Department of Resources and Development has at its head a very fine man who is highly qualified in his own profession, as an electrical engineer. By and large the technical personnel of that department have to do with construction, housing, the financing thereof and matters of that kind. I think it is a mistake to take a matter that definitely belongs in the Department of Agriculture and place it in the Department of Resources and Development, because I do not think we want to have the future of the agricultural industry of this country tied in with a lot of technicians who are already very much involved in problems they are finding it very difficult to solve.
On the other hand the minister at the head of the Department of Agriculture knows a great deal about agriculture and has for many years, both provincially and federally, administered legislation on the prairies and throughout the country that has had a specific relation to the subject matter of the resolution now before us. I think that is one point the government definitely should consider if they are going to embark upon a program of soil, land and water conservation as indicated in the speech from the throne. In my opinion the first thing they should determine is to place these measures under the jurisdiction of the department that is best able to deal with them, and I support the recommendation contained in the brief of the Nova Scotia farmers' association.
I do not want to go into detail, but over the years I have read quite a bit about the experience in the United States when they set up an organization apart from their department of agriculture and attempted to do the kind of job that it is suggested in the speech from the throne we are going to undertake to do apart from our Department of Agriculture. The government would be wise to read about the experience they had in the United States, because it left very much to be desired. I want to make that point, and I strongly urge the government to consider this matter and refer the whole problem to the Department of Agriculture.
Then I have a second recommendation to make to the government. For a great many years on the prairies we have had the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and there are many trained personnel who for a long time have been carrying on the type of work that is here visualized on a national scale. They have gained a great deal of experience. In order to obtain equality of development throughout the country, I believe that the government should consider at the earliest

possible date the possibility of extending the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to cover the whole country. I think in that act they have all of the powers necessary to go into a full scale program of conservation of water, land and forest, and of reclamation. 1 think that act covers the matter on a regional basis in a way that we desire for the whole of the country.
As is suggested in this resolution in my opinion there are only two things the government ought to consider. The first is keeping the problem in the hands of the Department of Agriculture, and the second is the extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act across the country with the necessary personnel to administer it in the other provinces. If that is done I think a base will be laid for a good over-all national development that would cover all the points suggested by the resolution now before the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) on stirring up so much discussion about a subject in which I am sure everyone has an interest. In my opinion it is more than an academic interest; it is a matter of the greatest importance to all of the people of this country. As the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) has pointed out, it is of the greatest importance to people everywhere, and I do not think there can be any disagreement between members on either side of the house about the desirability of conservation or even of a national policy.
The hon. member who introduced the resolution complained that members of other parties criticized the C.C.F. because they go in for planning. As I listened to him I found it very hard to disagree with the way he put his statement; but we do disagree with the C.C.F. for wanting to plan everything for us. In the course of his remarks, and I believe I am interpreting him correctly, he advocated a policy of nationalization of the soil, the forests and the things that grow in the soil, and I cannot agree with that.
This country has been wonderfully blessed by divine Providence with tremendous natural resources of soil, of forests and of water power; yet in almost every province from the Atlantic to the Pacific you hear complaints of shortages of one or another of them. I was told only yesterday that in the city of St. John's they are short of water, and that it is dangerous to extend the city any farther without making provision for additional water, for which they will have to go many miles. The federal government has advised investors in the United States
Conservation
that waters of the Yukon river cannot be diverted to develop an aluminum plant in Alaska because of the probable needs for development of water power within Canadian territory.
We are always hearing of tremendous floods and the soil erosion that follows those floods.
I remember reading of a very distinguished Newfoundlander, Sir Edmund Gosse, who became librarian of the British museum, and who wrote that when his father first went to Newfoundland 150 years ago at the site of the town of Harbour Grace great forests of spruce and pine grew down to the seashore. Today all the territory is a barren, and the word "barren" in Newfoundland has tremendous significance. It means vast stretches of land on which only small shrubbery grows. The government is now making an attempt to get trees to grow in that area.
When you consider that when this country was discovered, and for centuries afterwards, these great forests stretched over much more territory than they do today, and that despoliation by man, by forest fires sometimes caused by man's carelessness, and by insects has destroyed so much of it that we are worried about the future, then I think this resolution is timely in drawing the attention of hon. members and of important sections of the country to this problem.
These various resources are all related. I suppose the soil is the principal resource because from the soil the forests grow and the forests protect the water supply; but they are all interrelated. I would put the forests first in the sense that by having good forestry and reforestation, and by protecting the forests, we protect the waters in the lands where the forests are and in that way we protect the soil to a certain extent. In Newfoundland we have suffered terribly through forest fires, many of them caused by the railways. The substitution of oil-burning engines for the ordinary coal engines on the railways has had the splendid result of decreasing forest fires. When you pass along the railway line in Newfoundland or in the maritime provinces and see vast stretches of formerly beautiful forest lands destroyed, with nothing left but those gaunt spectres that stand up and seem to be protests against the wrongful use of the land by man, then we see that the need for protection and conservation is great.
Many years ago there was a man in Nova Scotia named Frank D. J. Barnjum-I do not know whether anyone here remembers him-who for years sent out letters to legislators and others warning them that the future would be disastrous if we kept on

Conservation
with the policy of using the forest resources without reforestation. I am glad to say that in recent years more attention has been given to the protection of forest lands in Newfoundland than was the case formerly. Every year now we have a fire prevention week or a forest protection week when attention is drawn to the preservation of the forests which mean so much to the people there. The same thing applies in the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec. By lectures to students, by broadcast talks, by notices and through the press the public is advised of the importance of the forests and the forest products industry to the country. This afternoon the hon. member for DufTerin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) told us something that is a fact, that the newsprint industry today is the most important industry from a monetary standpoint. It exceeds in the value of its production the whole of the agricultural industry; and that is a tremendous statement for anyone to make.
In Newfoundland we use the forests to obtain building material, fencing material, firewood, pit props and also pulp and paper. I suppose in the other maritime provinces the forests are used for the same purposes.
The hon. member for Kootenay West seemed to advocate nationalization, a nationally directed policy, but when he was talking about the work that was being done in the United States, which he praised, he spoke of co-operation between the federal government and the governments of the various states. It seems to me that what is desirable in this country is co-operation. The speech from the throne, in referring to conservation of the water resources of the country, speaks of co-operation between the federal government and the provinces. The measure, of which notice has been given by the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), implies co-operation and not a policy directed by the federal government. I do not think it would be advisable to have a policy directed from Ottawa. I believe it should be a matter of agreement, and the representatives of the different provinces and the federal government should get together.

In any case the federal government, through its ministers, could act in a liaison capacity to bring the representatives of the provinces together and pool their knowledge and experience, and in that way a policy could be worked out by agreement and not by direction.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I rise to support the resolution of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). I feel that he has done the country a service by proposing the resolution now before us, which requests that steps be taken to provide a national policy of soil, forest and water conservation and land use in Canada.
This afternoon I noticed that the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) seemed to think he was in the provincial legislature in Saskatchewan rather than in the House of Commons. He said something about a development program in the northeastern

part of Saskatchewan, and wished the Saskatchewan government would help develop that area in co-operation with the P.F.R.A. I am not well acquainted with the issues involved but so far as I know the Saskatchewan government has always been prepared to co-operate with the P.F.R.A. in every way possible. However, the government of Saskatchewan does not want to turn over that land to the sole administration of the P.F.R.A. So far as the Saskatchewan government is concerned, I feel it has taken an active and growing interest in conservation. This is borne out by the fact that the budget of the Saskatchewan department of agriculture has increased five times since 1943-44. In addition to that increase in the budget of the department of agriculture, $750,000 has been allocated to capital account, mainly for irrigation and drainage projects.
To me the matter of conservation is simply the matter of using the land and water resources in the best way possible. Any program of conservation for Canada is a program that will help all parts of this nation. In looking over the various reports that have been made by agricultural authorities, certainly the maritime provinces and Ontario stand to benefit a great deal from a conservation program. A committee of experts on land use, meeting in Guelph in 1942, reported that there were 8,000 square miles of abandoned farm land in the province of Ontario, and that at the then rate of rehabilitation it would take 800 years to bring that area back into crop production. I believe that Ontario, because of its high rainfall and its rolling topography, has probably suffered more from water erosion than any other part of Canada. For that reason Ontario has a stake in a national conservation program. I feel that a conservation program is something that will appeal to all Canadians in all parts of our country.
The best person to undertake the conservation of land is the farmer who is operating that land. It is unfair to expect the farmer unassisted to conserve for posterity his land resources when he must make a living from year to year. Perhaps because of heavy debt the farmer must work his land in such a way as to obtain the greatest possible annual income. From personal experience and observation I can say that the western Canadian farmer is not in a position to follow the best land use practices. Even though a given part of his farm, from the standpoint of conservation over a long period, might be better used in the production of grass, in most cases the farmer is unable to do that economically because he has a mortgage on his farm or has obtained some credit and his creditors are
Conservation
knocking at the door. They want cash every year, so he is forced to grow a cash crop. He is forced to raise grain year after year, even though he may know that such a practice is not the best long-term land use for his particular farm.
If the farmer is to conserve his land as he would like to do, and as he needs to in the national interest, then some assistance must be given that farmer. This principle has been amply demonstrated by the experience of the United States department of agriculture. In the United States a farmer is paid a specific sum for carrying out a specific conservation practice on his farm. If we want our farmers to engage in contour farming, in a proper system of crop rotation, then the farmers will need some financial assistance and leadership from the federal government.
The House of Commons does not have to take my word for that statement. I have before me the words of L. B. Thomson, director of the prairie farm rehabilitation organization. He makes the statement that if we are to get proper land use and proper conservation of our soil resources, then in addition to an educational program there must be some financial assistance provided to individual farmers to undertake necessary and specific conservation practices.
I feel that it is in the long-term interests of our nation to provide a conservation program for our soil resources, particularly when we are aware of the fact that from our land we obtain our greatest new wealth. Our soil produces new wealth annually to the amount of over $2 billion. From the standpoint of keeping our economy buoyant and maintaining prosperity in the nation we need to make sure that agricultural production is maintained, yes and even increased. If we fail as a nation to conserve our agricultural resources, in addition to the eroded lands of Ontario and the maritime provinces we may have a return to the dust bowl conditions that prevailed in the three prairie provinces in the 1930's, and when those conditions prevail over a long period of time they do permanent damage to the productivity of the soil.
One of the most powerful weapons for peace and democracy in the world today is food. It is difficult to see how we can promote democracy when we on the North American continent are worrying about burdensome agricultural surpluses and doing little about them, while at the same time most of the citizens of the world are hungry. I say that a program of proper conservation, a program of expansion of our food production, together with policies to make that production available to the hungry peoples of the

Conservation
world, would be our best and most effective contribution toward peace in the world.
I come from a province that has never had a surplus of water. Nevertheless we have one source of water that might be utilized more effectively in the future than it has been in the past. I refer to the Saskatchewan river, and specifically to the development of the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project. In moving this resolution the C.C.F. have not attempted to show that we are promoting conservation and others are not. The same is true in reference to the South Saskatchewan dam. If there is one person in Canada who has done perhaps more than anyone else to promote the idea of the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project and the benefits that would flow therefrom to all the people of Saskatchewan it is our own federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Ever since 1935 he has toured that province year in and year out, election after election, explaining to the people of Saskatchewan the great benefits that would flow from the development of the South Saskatchewan dam, and we agreed with him all the time. As the elections were held the Minister of Agriculture became more specific.

Over the years, and indeed for a number of years, the P.F.R.A. engineers have recommended this project. They have given their

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I am willing to postpone discussion of the report until it has been made public, although I want to say that my whole purpose in discussing it at this time is not to comment on its contents, but merely to point out that the people of Saskatchewan are demanding and will continue to demand the completion of the South Saskatchewan irrigation and development project.
The resolution of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) refers to the development of water, land and forest resources. If we are to conserve adequately our forests, our lands and our water resources there must be legislation to make this possible.

I should like to point out, however, that we shall oppose any move to take land conservation and use out of the Department of Agriculture and hand it over to the Department of Resources and Development, or any other department. Surely no group is better qualified to deal with the conservation of land resources than the persons who have specialized in the subject, and who have obtained university and technical knowledge in the field of land use and conservation.
I see on the order paper a resolution which forecasts legislation to provide for the conservation of water resources, for which the federal government will pay 37 J per cent in respect of any project. Let me say to the government that this measure should not mean that the present program under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, controlled by the Department of Agriculture, is curtailed in any way. I hope it does not mean that there will be either a quick or even a gradual shift to the Department of Resources and Development any part of the land conservation program now under the Department of Agriculture. We in this group do not always agree with the Minister of Agriculture and the officials in his department; but I think it is agreed by all that the prairie farm rehabilitation program has been good, that at least at the top it is staffed by most competent persons, that nothing should be done to curtail the program, but that rather everything should be done to expand it. If we use the present facilities it offers and, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has said, make it applicable to all parts of Canada, and use the personnel we now have in the Department of Agriculture, we shall have taken a long step forward in conserving our land and water resources.

Mr. Speaker, I have found this debate particularly interesting, and for that reason I feel grateful to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and to other hon. members who have taken part in it. Because, as has been said, it is not a party matter; rather it is a matter in which we have common interest. My own excuse for taking part in the debate is some of the observations that have been made during the course of the debate.
I was, in the first place, surprised and perhaps the least bit shocked, by what was said by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), that the standing committee of the house set up for the purpose of dealing with these matters has not been called together for a good many years. I have asked myself why that was so; and the answer I have given myself is that perhaps it has not seemed very urgent, that other things have
Conservation
seemed more urgent, and that this has been allowed more or less to remain in the background.
I should like to make one or two suggestions. First of all, this is an urgent matter. These are increasing evils. There is increasing deterioration going on at the present time which, if not stopped, will become extremely serious. In that connection I should like to refer to a report made some years ago under the auspices of the dominion and Ontario governments, I believe, with regard to a small area in Ontario which was intensively investigated.
Having regard to erosion and other matters which have been referred to here tonight, it seems to me if we look back to that time we see that during the war-and the report I mention was made at that time-there was every intention of dealing quite seriously with this problem when the war should end. It was felt that this and other forms of activity would be necessary to provide employment.
I think if we look back we can see clearly that what has happened in the last several years is that we have been so busy exploiting new resources, notably mineral resources which, after all, do not re-create themselves -"one toot and yer oot!"-that these resources have been neglected. These resources which, as has been pointed out today, are perennial, provided we do not destroy them, have tended to receive far less attention than they otherwise would.
This leads me to ask whether the situation is satisfactory or unsatisfactory. I was a good deal reassured by one thing said this afternoon by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) because, like the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), I remember the letters which used to be sent out 25 years ago by Mr. Barnjum. He, as I recall it, predicted disaster unless we very quickly pulled ourselves together in the matter of forest conservation. As I say, I was a good deal reassured this afternoon by what the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said, though at the same time he stressed in the strongest possible manner the need still for a proper kind of conservation.
Leaving the forests for the moment and speaking about agriculture, we are all only too familiar as we go through the country, whatever part we are from, with the spectacle of abandoned farms, particularly due to erosion. I suppose that would have been dealt with much more effectively than it has been if it were not that, in spite of all our failings and in spite of all our neglect, we have had so much virgin land and so many

Conservation
new resources. In connection with agriculture we have produced plenty for our own needs, and sometimes almost more than we felt we could find places in which to sell it. That seems to have been the reason for our neglect.
As to the extent of the neglect, I should like to read a sentence or two from a report I hold in my hand which was made about the Ganaraska watershed. The Ganaraska is a little river emptying into lake Ontario at Port Hope. Anyone who has passed through that farming country would be delighted with its appearance and surprised to learn that it was suffering from severe deterioration.
I should like to read briefly from the introduction to the report, which is signed by Dr. R. C. Wallace, one time principal of Queen's university and before that, as hon. members will recall, an Albertan, and before that a Manitoban. Certainly few people have greater knowledge of Canada than has Dr. Wallace. The introduction to the report is dated December 21, 1943, and in it Dr. Wallace says, in part:
Deterioration of soil, due in large measure to the removal of forest cover, has given rise to serious problems in many parts of Canada. The soundest and most economical methods must be found by which such land may be brought back into productive use. It is now well recognized that conservation projects should be included among the major enterprises, both for providing employment in the immediate post-war period and over the longer term, to help to stabilize the economy as a whole.
And later:
On any basis, conservation is a pressing need. It is far from sufficiently realized how urgent the task of soil conservation is. If southern Ontario, in which the Ganaraska region lies, be taken as one of the older areas of Canadian settlement, it was estimated twenty years ago that 8,500 square miles of land was marginal or submarginal for agriculture. Recent observations show that in spite of the expanded conservation programs of the government in recent years, the submarginal areas are growing larger.
And finally he says:
At the present rate at which remedial measures are being applied, it is estimated that it would take several hundred years to deal with the problem.
In other words the soil could be so robbed in a very few years that conservation would then entail a task lasting several hundred years. The problem is there, but of course nothing will be done about it unless we have a certain sense of urgency. Perhaps it will be said, "How are you going to have a sense of urgency about the growing of wheat when we have a so-called surplus of wheat?"
It seems to me that we have moved into an international situation where we have to have a sense of responsibility as well as a sense
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
of marketing. As a boy I can remember feeling that it was rather surprising and rather fortunate that we on this continent were so well off, that we were so much better off than the people in other crowded parts of the world such as Asia, about which we read. But I accepted that as being a fortunate chance that I had been born in Canada and that we Canadians had these advantages. I probably felt that all we had to do was to be thankful for them.
But I think we all feel that we have moved into a different stage of history with the shrinkage of the world, as someone said, to the size of a baseball. I think everyone will agree that we have moved into a situation where we cannot afford to be irresponsible in the use of the land that we have. I was talking recently to a man who had just come back from India, and he spoke of what a distressing experience he had had in seeing crowded populations who hardly knew what it was to have a square meal.
I am not forgetting the humanitarian point of view because I know we all have that, but I think we have moved into a situation where it will be not only our duty but our interest to see that our lands and resources are conserved, that we grow the greatest possible amount of food. I am not overlooking what may be the immediate problem of finding out how we can fit this into world trading relationships, what techniques we can adopt and what relationships can be brought about so that what is grown here can be made available.
I just wanted to place these few remarks on the record. I am not purporting to say what exact steps should be taken. I have no quarrel with the wording of the resolution, as I feel that in spite of whatever other preoccupations we have we should not allow this matter of conservation to escape our attention. If we do so, one of these days we may wake up and find that the other resources which now are doing so much to assist our economy may not be needed as much as they are at the moment, and that all these particular workings which we now have will one day have disappeared. But as was pointed out earlier this day in this house, through the providence of God the resources we are now talking about are without end if we as the human agents do our part to maintain them.

Mr. Speaker, I tried on one or two occasions before this to rise but it was not possible for me to get into the debate. I do not propose

to take up much time in repeating the arguments that have been used by speakers who have preceded me in an effort to convince the house that this resolution should pass. I shall try to limit myself to dealing with a few things which perhaps have not been stressed to any great extent.
In the first place, I want to let it be known that those for whom I speak favour very much the tenor of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). We think it is timely. We think one of the most important results accruing from the discussion of a resolution of this kind is to focus the attention of the people throughout the country on the absolute need for all kinds of conservation activity, whether it be in the field of conservation of the fertility of the soil, the prevention of erosion, the conservation of water resources, the conservation of our forest growth or whatever else it may be. We do feel that influencing public opinion is one of the few remaining areas of effective action that are open to us.
We believe in a private enterprise system; we fight to uphold it and to continue it, but I must point out that one of the weaknesses of the private enterprise system, at least in so far as conservation is concerned, is that when you once have alienated resources from the control of the crown you have parted with any effective action that a government can take to conserve what is there, at least without interfering unduly with what we consider to be the rights of private enterprise.
This is particularly true in the field of soil conservation because in this country we follow the practice of selling the land to private holders. Once a sale has been consummated it is practically impossible for a government to take any effective action to see that fertility is conserved. But we can focus the attention of the people upon the necessity of carrying out all kinds of conservation methods, and publicity to be obtained through a debate of this kind is one effective way of doing that job. There will have to be a great deal of educational effort. Perhaps it is in the field of education where the results of a resolution of this kind will be most felt. I am glad at this time to be able to add my voice to the voices of those who have already spoken in support of this resolution.
I should like to see action taken to initiate some form of dominion-provincial activity. Whether a conference is all that is needed is something I have not decided at the moment. I lean to the view that after a conference such as is envisioned in the resolution is called, after it has considered the whole field of conservation and has perhaps suggested
Conservation
some type of policy, if the work is going to be really effective there will have to be a continuing dominion-provincial commission of some sort to follow up the work. Such a commission could continue investigations and make reports to parliament on its activities every year to keep us informed and help us in turn to educate the people back home about the essential nature of the conservation work that has to be undertaken. Therefore I would suggest to the house that a joint dominion-provincial conservation commission be considered along with the conference that has been suggested in the resolution. Already there have been quite a number of demonstrations of dominion-provincial action, and effective action at that, in the conservation field. I recall being quite closely associated with one or more of them, and I should like to say a word or two in connection with the two or three that I have in mind.
In the early days of this century it came to the attention of farsighted men in western Canada that something would have to be done to preserve the watersheds on the east slope of the Rocky mountains in the province of Alberta if we were ever to conserve and control the water flow and prevent the denuding of the forests, which of course would result in the drying up of the wellsprings of the great streams that flow across the western prairies. As a consequence of the farsighted recommendations of these men about 1910 or 1911, if I remember correctly, action was taken to set up what came to be known as the Rocky mountain forest reserve. That occupied an area of somewhere between 15,000 and 17,000 square miles. The area started at the northern boundary of Waterton lakes park and extended northward along the foothills of the Rockies to the northern boundary of about the 60th township. The area is all forest.
After the setting up of the reserve in 1911, efforts were then made to prevent forest fires ravaging the timber, and to try to conserve the growth as much as possible so the watersheds would be preserved. When the resources were handed over to the province of Alberta in 1931 an effort was made to interest the federal government in some dominion-provincial arrangement for protecting the watersheds. Not much was accomplished, however, until about 1938 or 1939, when I recall having made several trips to Ottawa from Edmonton, along with certain other ministers, to talk to the federal officials. At that time we took the position that the only effective way to conserve and preserve the watersheds of the eastern slope of the Rockies was to arrange some form of joint dominion-provincial activity and agreement.

Conservation
We tried our best to interest the people in the western provinces as well as those in the east in our problem, but it was not until about 1947 that other farsighted men began to see the importance of entering into a form of agreement with the province.
In 1947 the dominion government and the provincial government of Alberta set up what came to be known as the eastern Rockies forest conservation board which was given authority to administer the whole area of the east slope of the Rockies and take whatever action might be necessary to preserve watersheds, build roads, provide fire protection, provide for the cutting of the timber where it became too thick, in fact in practice all branches of conservation and preservation. The work that has been done by the joint commission has been most commendable and effective. We feel that it offers an excellent demonstration of what can be accomplished by dominion-provincial co-operation, and we are certain that the continued flow of the rivers, particularly the North Saskatchewan and the South Saskatchewan and their tributaries, depends upon the successful conservation of the eastern slope of the Rockies.
No one knows how much that sort of cooperation has meant to the western provinces, even beyond the boundaries of the province of Alberta where the conservation project lies. We feel that, by preserving the watersheds through joint action of the dominion and the province, all the western provinces are going to benefit, and I am satisfied that in due course the waters now needed so badly in the dry lands of southern Saskatchewan will be made available as a consequence of that conservation. There is one example. It seems to me that what was accomplished in that instance can be extended into other fields.
There is another example I should like to mention. Several speakers have already referred to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and what it has done. That act of course is the sole responsibility of the federal government. There is a considerable amount of co-operation with the provinces in certain phases of administration; but what we should like to see, in addition to the extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to cover all Canada, is a little more inclination to take the provinces into the confidence of the federal government and let them help to make policy; because anything that touches so vital a spot in the provinces as does rehabilitation and conservation ought to be of concern to the provinces, and they should have some say in the formation of policy. They could have such a say under the proposed joint commission on conservation that I

have already suggested, and I believe the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act could be made much more workable and effective if it were considered in the light of close cooperation between the two governments.
In the field of irrigation there has been a great deal of close co-operation between the province in which I live and the dominion government. Irrrigation projects and their development in southern Alberta have meant so much to our province and its economy, in fact so much to the whole economy of Canada, that a person could talk about them for a long time. Some of these irrigation schemes have been built as joint dominion-provincial projects, the two governments sharing the costs and the province taking the full responsibility for the colonization and management of the projects after they have been built. These projects have been very successful. Irrigation, in addition to making it possible to produce things on land that otherwise would not produce very much under dry conditions, does go further and succeeds to a very great measure in conserving the fertility of the soil. In any successful irrigation district in southern Alberta you will find that the fertility of the soil is being maintained and that erosion has been cut down to a minimum. Certainly wind erosion is very small compared with what it used to be. Not only that, but the farmers are practising the most intensive forms of conservation of the fertility of the soil. I imagine that with the present form of management of those irrigated lands we can expect them to continue producing in abundance for a great many years to come.
When I was in Germany in 1948 I went down into an area near Helmstedt on the autobahn, where the autobahn crosses the border into the east zone, and I visited some farms in that area. There was one especially where I had a chance to talk to the owner of the farm, and he said that the land he was farming had been in the possession of his family for nearly 400 years. The family had quite a history, and he said the very land that he was cropping sugar beets on then had been raising sugar beets successfully since the time of Napoleon. It is still producing 15 tons to the acre per year. That seemed to me, Mr. Speaker, to be an excellent example of real conservation of the fertility of the soil. It has only been accomplished because the people who were operating the land and who owned it valued it highly enough so they have been prepared to take whatever action was possible to see that erosion did not take place, to see that the fertility was not mined out of it, and that sort of thing.

There is this to be said about the land in Germany. The government did take a real interest in it and in every way possible did impress on the people of the country the necessity of using the most up-to-date methods, machinery, fertilizer, crop rotation and other conservation aids. As my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) says, the production of sugar beets, certainly in that instance, has been one of the best methods of conserving the fertility of the soil in that country. The same thing can be said of those areas in southern Alberta which have been producing sugar beets for as long as I can remember, and my memory goes back almost to the turn of the century. They have been raising sugar beets in southern Alberta that long, and some of those lands are still producing excellent crops of sugar beets and other things which the farmers use in their rotation program.
I merely wanted to mention that, Mr. Speaker, for the reason that wherever people can be made to see how important it is to preserve the fertility of the soil, and wherever they are given the information on which to build their programs; and at the same time wherever they are given an opportunity to produce those things which are best suited to the soil, then conservation results as a natural consequence of care in handling.
But it seems to me we are becoming pretty careless. As I understand from the debates that have been going on here since the session opened, we are letting the beet sugar industry languish. We are not doing what we should do to protect it. We are not doing what we can to see that a market with lucrative prices is there for the producers of sugar. If we allow that industry to go by default and be destroyed then, Mr. Speaker, we are deliberately taking steps to destroy the fertility of our soil; and all the conservation methods in the world which we might use would not restore it or bring it back.
Therefore I appeal to all concerned to weigh these things very, very carefully and see to it that whatever action we take as a federal government does not destroy the incentive to use care to preserve the resources with which God has blessed this great country. I would suggest by every means possible that the provincial and federal governments come to some agreement with respect to a national conservation policy in all these fields. Following the drafting of such a policy a joint dominion-provincial commission on conservation should be set up to report to this house regularly, and to make proposals for legislation that might be made effective by dominion-provincial action.
