speechtext:
I am very happy, Mr. Speaker, to have been fortunate enough to catch your eye on a matter of such general interest and importance. I am sure most of the members of this house would like to have an opportunity of saying a word, and I assure you that I will not speak long enough to prevent any other member from joining in the debate. However, I do want to deal with one or two points arising out of this particular resolution.
I have not had the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of hearing all of the interesting contributions that have been made to this debate, but I have listened with a great deal of interest to those which have been made while I have been able to be in the house this afternoon and this evening. It is quite obvious that there is unanimous agreement in this house on both the importance and the necessity of as broad a conservation program as is possible in this country.
When one looks at the variety and wealth of our natural resources, Mr. Speaker, one might think that we in Canada would be justified in having a tendency to be a little bit prodigal in our use of those resources. I am sure all will agree with me that in the past we have not been free from some grounds for complaint about the way our resources have been employed, and in some instances about a lack of thought for the future and lack of arrangements for conservation. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that besides doing a very creditable job in the manner in which we have developed and used our natural resources, in this country we have done a very creditable job in a number of directions in the field of conservation.
It has struck me during this debate that almost every member who has spoken has referred to one or more instances of important programs of conservation which are going on in his own area or of which he has personal knowledge. The western members have spoken of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the work that is being done under that legislation. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) who has just taken his seat has spoken of several other important matters of which he has personal knowledge. In the maritime provinces, for instance, we know of the excellent work that is being done under the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, a program which is bringing back into productive use much valuable land in the maritime provinces which had been won from the sea generations ago by the early settlers and which to a large extent had through neglect gone back to the sea. A great deal of the damage which had been done has been

Conservation
repaired and those lands are going to be a source of wealth and a resource for future generations.
In saying that much has been done one should not suggest that anything more than a very good start has been made in this country in the field of conservation of all our resources, forests, soil and water. My only complaint with the wording of the resolution which is before the house is that it calls for a dominion-provincial conference on conservation. It seems to me that at this stage the responsibility of this house, and of the government, is to make sure that we have a sound and effective program of conservation in all the fields which lie in the authority and responsibility of this federal government. We should bring into effect, so far as is reasonably possible, the kind of long-term programs which we believe will carry out our responsibilities in the fields in which we are obviously responsible.
I believe the announcement in the speech from the throne at the opening of this session of the government's plans for bringing forward conservation measures indicates that this government is acting in the manner in which I think it should act. It seems to me that a resolution of this house which would indicate to the nation that an immediate dominion-provincial conference on conservation should be called is premature, and would not contribute materially to the objectives which we all have in view.
I believe one proof of the point I am making is that a good many of the members who have taken part in this debate have, as I mentioned earlier, referred to the various fields of conservation of which they have knowledge, and have indicated that in those programs there is an effective and satisfactory element of co-operation between the federal authority and the provincial authorities involved. Certainly that is true of the particular program with which I am most familiar, the maritime marshland rehabilitation program. This is a joint program between the federal authority and the provinces. The federal government has taken the initiative and has supplied the greatest part of the money, equipment and technical personnel to do this work, but it has been a fine effort of co-operation.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the existence of that co-operation at the present time indicates that what is needed at the moment is not the calling of a conference, but steady progress along the lines on which we are already embarked. I should think that in the years to come, when further progress has been made, it may then be advisable to consider the calling of some sort of dominion-provincial conference. But so long as there

are important fields of endeavour in which we could make substantial progress, and in which we are receiving, and can be confident of continuing to receive the amount of useful co-operation that is required, I believe that it would not be necessary for this house to pass a resolution demanding the calling of a dominion-provincial conference.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I indicate my wholehearted support of the principle of conservation, and my belief that these objectives will be fulfilled, but indicate at the same time my criticism of this resolution in its demand for that particular type of conference at this time.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that together with several other members of this house I had the opportunity last week of having a conference with the members of the executive of the Nova Scotia association of agriculture. This is a very active body representing the farmers of Nova Scotia, who invited the members of this house from that province to meet with them. I was one of those fortunate enough to be able to attend. At that time they presented to us a brief, to which reference was made earlier in this debate by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). One of the important recommendations in that brief dealt with this matter of conservation. It is a matter in which they are vitally concerned, and upon which they have had a great deal of discussion. They are anxious for progress to be made in the field of conservation, and the burden of their recommendation was that their studies indicated that in other countries where conservation programs were satisfactory, so far as soil conservation was concerned, they were carried out by the Department of Agriculture.
My views are that the problems of conservation are matters with which we must cope, and the only kind of action any sensible person can wish to have is effective action. I am sure this government will study the problems of bringing effective action to bear on the matter of soil conservation, the conservation of water and forest resources, and if it is found that the only effective and sensible way in which this matter can be dealt with is under the Department of Agriculture, then it will be done in that way. My study of the problem has not been sufficient to convince me just what the proper answer is, but I can assure all those in my province who are interested in the matter that it will receive the most careful attention, and that any proposals that are put forward will be formulated on the basis of a sincere and carefully thought out policy intended to achieve the objectives which we all have in

view with the greatest possible speed, and with due regard to efficiency and economy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I believe it is safe to say that all members of this house have welcomed this debate. From time to time it is refreshing to get away from the problems of the troubled world to give some attention to the position of our people at home, and to the future of this country. I think we are all optimistic about that. We know that we have a very large country. We know that it is a country that has been very bountifully endowed with natural resources, and we know that we have a position that is being recognized in the world today although there are only 14 million of us here at the moment. But that does not mean that this nation is going to remain a nation of 14 million people. In 1901 we had a population of 5J million. I will not be here to register my surprise, but I would venture the prediction that those who know what is going on in Canada at the present time will be disappointed if by the census of 2001 there are' not 35 or 40 million people in this country. There is room for them and for a lot more. There is wealth for them and for a lot more, still undeveloped. But we must be careful and see that it is properly conserved, so that when our grandchildren, our great grandchildren and their grandchildren are members of a nation of many more millions than there are in this country at the present time there will still be enough of these natural resources to enable them to enjoy the kind of life we in this country can enjoy when the world is at peace.
I have been concerned with some of the publications that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) referred to and of which I took note. There is one more that I would call to his attention, a very interesting book published in the course of last summer by a forestry engineer of Quebec, Mr. Thomas Maher, entitled "Land of Milk and Honey or Wilderness of Cain". There are some parts of it with which I do not agree, but there are useful lessons one can learn from perusing it attentively.
We have made some mistakes; we have some abandoned farms; we have some places that might be in a different condition if other or somewhat different methods had been adopted in respect of them, but these are rather local problems. On the over-all picture we are not doing too badly. Last August I went up to lake St. John in the province of Quebec. There is a company up there marketing aluminum metal at the rate of $150 million worth a year, and all of our natural resources that are going into it
Conservation
are Canadian labour and electricity produced by the running water of our Canadian streams.
Then I went out to the west coast and stopped off at Trail. It will be recalled that 25 years ago there was an international dispute over the damage which farmers of the adjoining state of Washington, I think it is, claimed was caused to the vegetation in their state by the obnoxious fumes from the chimneys of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. There are no scars to show damage to any vegetation at the present time. Things grow out there, and they grow fast, and all traces of damage caused in that period have now disappeared. Since then those fumes have been applied to phosphate rock brought in from Montana, and the combination of the obnoxious fumes and the phosphate rock is $25 million worth of fertilizer a year; and every ton of that fertilizer, under normal growing conditions, means twelve additional tons of cereal crops.
Then I had the privilege of spending several hours each day for five days in the air over the mainland and over the island of Vancouver. I was tremendously impressed by the density and extent of the forest wealth of that Pacific coast, and rather felt that in spite of the large lumbering operations that have been carried on out there for so many years, and are still being carried on, we are not making any very great inroads into the forest wealth of that west coast. Perhaps my impression was somewhat strengthened by the fact that they were just about to open a $40 million pulp and paper plant at Campbell River where they are going to use nothing but refuse, sawdust, edgings, things that before were thrown away. That is an example of an improvement in our methods. We were wasteful, I think, in not making use of these things before, but we are getting over that.
Then I flew over to Edmonton and saw the tremendous progress that is being made on the petro-chemical plant. They are going to use waste there, too. I understand that before crude oil is used it has to go through refineries, and in the refining process there are some elements that do not go into the oil that is marketable. I had seen that in Sarnia, where there is a refinery where the waste goes from the oil refinery to the Polymer Corporation to make rubber, and that portion of the elements of that waste that is not taken to make the rubber goes over to the Dow Chemical Company for plastics and other commodities. Nothing is wasted but the little smell that you notice in the atmosphere. These are some of the things that are being done, and they rather convince

Conservation
one that we are becoming more careful, and that general conservation methods are being applied.
Of course when you come to deal with any specific item of natural resources you find that is something that belongs to the provinces and about which they are very jealous. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), when he was premier of Ontario, attended a dominion-provincial conference here and I remember-and I just looked it up to see how correct my memory was- that he enumerated the responsibilities of the provinces and what the provinces were doing, and the trained forces of civil servants they had built up to do that. I have no doubt that he remembers it, too. It is to be found on page 589 of the proceedings of the conference of 1945. After enumerating some other things he had this to say about natural resources:
Ours is the responsibility for the development of the vast resources which made production possible in this country during the war. Nothing that the dominion government did. nor has been called upon to do in the past in the way of technical development, laid the foundation for that huge production from the natural resources. That was the result of the development and supervision of these resources by the provincial governments throughout the years.
He described other provincial responsibilities, and went on to say:
I have only touched a part of the field that, until the compact of confederation is torn to pieces -and I too use the word compact-must be the responsibility of the provinces. Until the compact of confederation is torn to pieces, and please God it never will be, but until that is done, if these things are to be done at all they must be done by the provincial government. And to do these things, since long before confederation, the provincial governments have been building up skilled, highly trained and unselfish civil service organizations to carry out these great public responsibilities.
Well, here I rather shy away from using the expression "national policy" in connection with things of that kind. There are people who think that, when you use the term "national policy", there is some way in which the central authority is going to reach out and try to draw to itself some of the provincial jurisdiction. We do not want to do that. We want to have this country continue under the constitution that was set up, and we do want to co-operate with the provinces. There have been many declarations in the course of this debate of the extent to which this co-operation is working to the advantage of the whole Canadian public at the present time. There is on the order paper now a resolution to have enabling legislation which would permit the dominion government to co-operate and collaborate with the provinces in connection with the

conservation of water resources. There is the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which has provided a method whereby there was co-operation between the central and provincial governments on smaller, more localized projects.
Well, we want to create an atmosphere that will remove this fear that there is any attempt by the central government, whatever party may be in power, to reach out and take away from provincial administrations the responsibilities and jurisdiction which, by the constitution, are theirs.
I have not quite the same misgivings as the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) about the terms of this resolution. It asks that we consider calling a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a greater degree of collaboration and co-operation. Well, we are quite prepared to consider that. But we do not think it would be apt to produce very great results to do it right away or to do it on any wide scale. Let us continue to demonstrate, by the co-operation that will be taking place, that there are no ulterior motives in doing it, and that it is merely a genuine desire of Canadian citizens, to whatever administration they belong, to help the Canadian people of this generation discharge the responsibility they have to Canadian people of future generations to see that the resources of this country are not depleted, but are maintained, and will be available to be used by them, and will have increased productivity as the size of our population increases.
I think we can accept this recommendation that consideration be given to that. But I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) would himself agree that it would be better to have the house give consideration to this enabling provision, so that when we have a conference with them we can say to them, "The Canadian parliament has authorized us to go thus far with you to help you take the proper measures for the conservation of water resources".
I fully agree with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) that the conservation of water resources depends upon proper forest cover over a large part of the soil of Canada. The hon. member said this was an industry that contributed largely to the federal exchequer; but it is also the property of the provincial governments and makes very substantial contributions to the revenues of those provincial governments. I am sure they are very jealous of their control over the policies that are to be in force and carried on.
The hon. member has had much more experience than I with what is going on in that connection; but I think we would both

feel that the provincial governments have been doing very well, and that they have been enacting and administering pretty wise legislation for the proper management of their property, their forests on which they grant cutting rights, evidently renewable but cutting rights, only. The hon. member said that this goes on. I know that up in the lake St. John district, where I was, it has been going on now for a century, and that there are now growths that are better and more productive than the first that were taken off those same lands.
That is something that is progressive. We do not find in one year, or even in one decade, the situation they have in Sweden. It is the result of experience, and experience means trial and error. Some mistakes are made. Mistakes are corrected. You add one satisfactory experience to another satisfactory experience.
On the whole I think the warnings given by those who have written about the depletion of our resources are good and healthy warnings; but they must not induce too deep a pessimism in any of us. Because I do think that, given peace in our days, the management of the resources of this country is going to be sufficiently wise to enable us to look forward to a very substantial increase in population, without feeling that there are not going to be enough of those resources available for those generations to exploit and pass on to the generation that will follow them.
Once again, to all those who have taken part in this debate I hope I may, without sounding at all impertinent, offer congratulations, even thanks. I do so because I think it is a good thing from time to time in this troubled world, with all the international problems we worry about, to give some thought and attention to the brighter side of the picture, and to quicken somewhat that desire we have to do what appears to be necessary as our part toward preserving peace in our day, so that the conservation policies being applied and developed, and which should be expanded, will be productive of those results for the future generations which so many of us say, and so often, seem to have been in the designs of Providence for the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate, but some of the things said have made me feel that perhaps one more matter should be brought to the attention of the house and country.
It has been conveyed to me, on what I consider good authority, that about the only way we can be really sure of retaining the 68108-59
Conservation
fertility of the soil is through having introduced into the soil from time to time organic matter from animals. I have been told that one may put fertilizers-nitrates, phosphates, and the rest of them-on the soil, and probably force a crop, but that ultimately soil bacteria will play a part which we must not overlook in the retention of soil fertility.
Having laid down this general principle, which I believe to be sound, I would draw the attention of the house and country once again to what I consider a dangerous trend in this nation in respect of the dairy industry. I am afraid we are neglecting that industry in a way which will probably cast upon us a certain amount of reflection in the minds of those who succeed us. People these days are so anxious to save five cents-practically all of us are that way-that they are ready to use margarine freely rather than pay additional money for butter. By reason of that fact it looks as though our dairy industry is going to suffer seriously. There are signs that this result has occurred and is occurring to a greater degree.
It has been brought to my attention that notwithstanding the introduction of margarine there are more dairy stock in Canada per capita than we had before we started using margarine. I am not just sure what may be the significance of that fact. It may be that the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease and certain other factors have entered into the matter, but if we continue to use the products of vegetable oils instead of butter I cannot see how our dairying industry can be maintained in the healthy condition it was in before we began using margarine and vegetable oils so freely.
I am quite sure that nearly everybody wishes he knew the solution. I am not prepared to suggest what is the solution. I believe that two provinces in our nation have forbidden the use of margarine. I am not quite ready to agree with what they have done, though it may be found in the long run that they have been wise in their decision. It has been suggested that subsidies be paid to help the dairy industry. I have not given the matter sufficient study and thought to be able to feel competent to make any recommendation in that respect.
But I do make this observation once more, that we in Canada should most earnestly study ways and means whereby we can have a greater number of dairy cows. It must be borne in mind that it will be quite impossible to conserve the fertility of our soil for future generations, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has so admirably expressed it, unless we have a large number of livestock on our farms.

Conservation
As a minor illustration of how serious this may be may I say that I suppose most hon. members have lived in a time when horses instead of tractors were used on our farms. Everyone knows that by the use of horses we were returning fertility to the soil in several ways. But now we no longer use horses as formerly and as a consequence that amount of fertility is not being returned to the soil. We operate barren tractors today, and the only thing that goes on the land is some burned oil which is more likely to impair the effectiveness of soil bacteria, or even destroy them, than to help them.
We cannot, afford to fail to take cognizance of all these facts as we contemplate a policy for conserving the fertility of the soil. I feel
that I have made my contribution, and it is this: we simply must give more attention to the preservation of our dairy industry.
On motion of Mr. Hodgson the debate was adjourned.
